items.title: "My idea of a Netflix for games doesn’t work": Garry's Mod creator says struggling spiritual successor S&box will go free to play as part of major rethink
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: Earlier this year, Garry's Mod and Rust developers Facepunch Studios released S&box, a mix of open source game development platform/spiritual successor to
items.text:
Earlier this year, Garry's Mod and Rust developers Facepunch Studios released S&box, a mix of open source game development platform/spiritual successor to their Valve prop-filled physics sandbox. It's not fared well, only earning mixed reviews and being stuffed with low quality AI generated games early doors. Now, Facepunch founder Garry Newman has announced plans for a major overhaul that'll see S&box go free to play.

"I’ve been rethinking what s&box should look like over the past couple of weeks," Newman wrote in an announcement post put up on Steam and the game's website. "The platform is not well liked, it doesn’t have good retention. I’m embarrassed by our reviews, I am ashamed. Listening to all the negative feedback, absorbing, taking it seriously and deciding what we should and shouldn’t be doing. It’s not a big secret that it hasn’t been going well.

"Our focus has been on the engine and the development experience. That’s what we love, that’s what turns us on - but we’re not selling an engine, we’re selling a game. So we need to do much much better on the game, we need to shift our focus to what players are experiencing, not developers. Part of this focus is drawing our attention to the Sandbox Game. Giving it parity with the Garry’s Mod version and surpassing it. Showing everyone what the engine can do, adding more NPCs, adding vehicles, offering a first class multiplayer experience, supporting addons and customisation."

Newman went on to acknowledge that the way Facepunch went about setting up S&box as a Roblox-esque hub of user-created games hasn't gone as hoped, something quickly knocked together AI generated games hasn't helped. Though, the developer seems to see S&box's core philosophy in terms of game curation as more of a root cause than the proliferation of AI that's contributed by making it "much much harder" to make sure good quality games float to the top.

"My idea of a Netflix for games doesn’t work," he admitted. "It’s not feasible. It’s not how people discover games. You can’t land people on a menu of 60 games and say have fun. That’s not a good experience. People want to find games through recommendations, through active multiplayer games, through watching streamers, influencers and content creators. We have been coming at it from the wrong direction. We shouldn’t strive to be a platform with the most games available. We should strive to be a platform with the best, most popular games available."

So, Facepunch are making a bunch of changes which include swapping out S&box's weird cartoony "citizen" character models for standard human ones, which'll certainly make the game look less Robloxy. The most noteworthy tweak, however, is that it'll be going free to play "towards the end of the year". Newman wrote that this was always the route his studio planned to take S&box down eventually, but the view that attracting more players is more important than earning cash on the door in addition to via in-game skin sales has led them to take that plunge early. "Everyone who has paid for the game will automatically get a bunch of exclusive steam inventory items (extra if you bought it at $20 vs $10) that I hope will justify the purchase price," the dev added.

Those are far from the only changes planned as part of what Newman and co have branded a rethink of S&box, so it's well worth reading the full post if you want the full picture of everything Facepunch are doing as part of this effort to push the game onto a more favourable trajectory. It certainly has a lot of ground to make up if it's ever to become anywhere near as beloved as GMod or Rust, but Newman certainly doesn't seem afraid to confront missteps he's spearheaded, which is a start.

items.author: Hannah Hunt

items.text:
Disney’s relationship with Fortnite has already put some of its biggest characters into the game's bonkers playground. Marvel heroes and Star Wars villains can share a match without anyone needing to explain how their universes collided. Those collaborations helped establish Epic Games as a place where Disney could reach players beyond traditional adaptations of its movies.

The companies made that relationship considerably bigger in February 2024, when Disney announced a $1.5 billion investment in Epic alongside plans for a connected games and entertainment universe. The project promised experiences drawing from properties including Marvel and Star Wars, with opportunities to play and create. It was an ambitious pitch, even for companies already accustomed to working with enormous audiences.

Epic is now reportedly directing staff to use an “AI-first” development process on an unannounced Disney shooter featuring Marvel and Star Wars characters. According to new reports, an internal message instructed developers to use “no more handwritten code” and said the game’s art would be produced through AI workflows. The report describes humans guiding that work, with tools including Anthropic’s Claude involved in production.

Collider Exclusive · Sci-Fi Personality Quiz
Which Sci-Fi Hero Are You Most Like?
Paul Atreides · Captain Kirk · Princess Leia · Ellen Ripley · Max Rockatansky

Five iconic heroes. Five completely different ways of facing an impossible universe. One of them shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of refusing to back down. Eight questions will tell you which one.

🏜️Paul Atreides

🖖Capt. Kirk

✊Princess Leia

🔦Ellen Ripley

🔥Max Rockatansky

FIND YOUR HERO →

01

How do you lead when the stakes couldn't be higher?
The way you lead under pressure is the most honest thing about you.

AI absorb everything — every variable, every pattern — and move only when I know the path forward.
BI read the room, make the call, and own the consequences. Hesitation costs more than mistakes.
CI rally people. A cause needs a voice, and I refuse to let fear be louder than conviction.
DI assess the threat, establish what needs doing, and get it done without waiting for permission.
EI don't lead. I act. Others can follow or not — I'm already moving.

NEXT QUESTION →

02

What is your greatest strength in a crisis?
The quality that keeps you alive when everything else fails.

APrescience — the ability to see further ahead than anyone else and plan accordingly.
BImprovisation — I'm at my best when the plan falls apart and I have to invent a new one.
CConviction — I know what I'm fighting for, and that certainty doesn't waver under fire.
DComposure — I stay functional when everyone around me is falling apart. Panic is a luxury.
EEndurance — I outlast things. I take the hit and keep moving long after others have stopped.

NEXT QUESTION →

03

What is the thing you'd sacrifice everything else for?
Your deepest motivation is your truest compass.

AThe survival and dignity of my people — even if I have to become something frightening to ensure it.
BThe safety of my crew — every single one of them. No one gets left behind.
CFreedom — for my people, for every world still crushed under the weight of an empire.
DThe truth — what actually happened, what's actually out there, whether anyone believes me or not.
EThe one person — or the one memory — that still makes any of this worth surviving for.

NEXT QUESTION →

04

How do you relate to the people around you?
Who you are to others under pressure is who you really are.

AWith intensity and distance — I care deeply, but the weight I carry makes closeness complicated.
BWith warmth and irreverence — I take the mission seriously, not myself.
CWith directness and trust — I say what I mean, and I expect the people I work with to rise to it.
DWith professional care but clear limits — I'll protect you, but I won't pretend we're family.
EWith wariness that slowly becomes loyalty — I don't trust easily, but when I do, it holds.

NEXT QUESTION →

05

You're facing a threat that no one else believes is real. What do you do?
How you respond when you're the only one who sees it defines everything.

APrepare in silence. If they won't listen, I'll be ready when they finally have to.
BKeep pushing until someone listens — and if no one does, handle it myself.
CBuild the case, find the allies, and make the threat impossible to ignore.
DDocument everything. The truth matters even if no one believes it yet.
EStop trying to convince anyone. Survive it. That's the only argument that counts.

NEXT QUESTION →

06

What has your heroism cost you personally?
Every hero pays. The question is what — and whether they'd pay it again.

AMy innocence — I've seen what I'm capable of, and I can't unsee it.
BPeople I loved — the command chair has a view, but it's a lonely one.
CA normal life — I gave up everything ordinary the moment I chose the cause.
DMy sense of safety — I know exactly what's out there now, and I can't pretend otherwise.
EAlmost everything — and I'm still not sure what I'm carrying it all for. But I keep going.

NEXT QUESTION →

07

How do you feel about the rules of the world you're in?
Every hero has a relationship with the system. What's yours?

AI understand them deeply — and I know exactly which ones must be broken, and why.
BI respect the spirit of them and bend the letter when the situation demands it.
CThe system is the problem. I'm not here to work within it — I'm here to dismantle it.
DI follow protocol until protocol stops being useful. Then I make the call myself.
EThe rules collapsed a long time ago. What's left is instinct, and mine are reliable.

NEXT QUESTION →

08

When everything is on the line, what keeps you going?
The answer is the most honest thing about you.

ADestiny — or something that feels so much like it that the difference no longer matters.
BThe people on my ship — their faces, their trust, the fact that they're counting on me.
CThe belief that what we're fighting for is worth every sacrifice, including this one.
DSheer refusal to let it win — whatever it is. I don't stop. That's just who I am.
EI'm not sure anymore. But the road is still there, and I'm still on it.

REVEAL MY HERO →

Your Hero Has Been Identified
Your Sci-Fi Hero Is…

Your answers point to the iconic sci-fi hero who shares your instincts, your values, and your particular way of facing the impossible.

Arrakis · Dune

Paul Atreides

You carry a weight most people would crumble under — the knowledge of what you're capable of, and the burden of what you might have to become.

You see further ahead than others and you plan accordingly, even when the vision frightens you.

You are driven by loyalty to your people and a sense of destiny you didn't ask for but can't escape.

Paul Atreides is not simply a hero — he is someone who understands the cost of power and chooses to bear it anyway.

That gravity, that willingness to carry what others won't, is exactly you.

USS Enterprise · Star Trek

Captain Kirk

You lead with instinct, warmth, and an absolute refusal to accept a no-win scenario — because you've always believed there's a third option nobody else has thought of yet.

You take the mission seriously without ever taking yourself too seriously.

Your crew would follow you anywhere, not because you demand it, but because you've earned it.

Kirk's genius isn't tactical — it's human. He reads people, bends rules with purpose, and wills outcomes into existence through sheer conviction.

That combination of warmth, audacity, and relentless optimism is unmistakably yours.

The Rebellion · Star Wars

Princess Leia

You are the kind of person who holds the line when everyone else is losing faith — not because you're fearless, but because giving up simply isn't something you're capable of.

You lead through conviction. Your voice carries because your belief is unshakeable.

You gave up everything ordinary the moment you chose the cause, and you've never looked back.

Leia is not a supporting character in her own story — she is the moral centre of the entire rebellion.

That same fierce, principled, unbreakable core is what defines you.

The Nostromo · Alien

Ellen Ripley

You are not reckless, not grandiose, and not particularly interested in being anyone's hero — you just refuse to stop when it matters.

You see threats clearly, you document the truth even when no one listens, and when the time comes you handle it yourself.

Ripley's heroism is earned, not performed. She doesn't have a speech — she has a flamethrower and a plan.

You share her composure under the worst possible pressure, and her refusal to pretend the monster isn't there.

When it counts, you don't flinch. That's everything.

The Wasteland · Mad Max

Max Rockatansky

You have been through fire that would break most people — and what came out the other side is something the world underestimates at its peril.

You don't ask for help, don't need validation, and don't wait for anyone to tell you the rules no longer apply.

Your loyalty, when it finally arrives, is absolute — but it's earned in silence and tested in action, not in words.

Max is not a nihilist. He is someone who lost everything and found, against his will, that he still has something worth protecting.

That bruised, stubborn, ultimately human core is exactly yours.

↻ RETAKE THE QUIZ

Epic Says Its Developers Will Remain the Creative Drivers

Image via Epic Games

The reported instructions go considerably further than using AI for an occasional task. They would make generated material central to both the game’s code and its art, with developers responsible for directing and managing the results. Bloomberg reports that some staff members were stunned by the announcement, which followed slower-than-expected progress and an underestimate of the staffing required. That puts the proposed production change alongside an existing development problem. Epic’s public response emphasizes the people overseeing the technology.

A spokesperson told the publication that the company is embracing AI-accelerated development while describing Epic’s developers as its creative drivers. CEO Tim Sweeney also acknowledged a broader push toward AI, saying staff was being moved around to support it. He framed the goal as increasing what employees could build, rather than doing the same work with fewer people. The frustrating part is that Epic reportedly underestimated how many developers the project needed, and its answer is to put AI at the center of production. The people hired to make the game would instead be expected to guide the generated work and fix whatever comes back wrong. Generating something faster doesn’t make it worth using, and checking that output still takes time and expertise.

Calling the process “AI-first” does nothing to explain why it would produce a better game than giving developers the resources they needed in the first place. Published Oct 14, 2026, 4:00 AM EDT

Nicholas Becher is a gaming journalist with an MFA in Creative Writing from FAU. With extensive experience playing video games, he covers all forms of gaming content at Screen Rant, from breaking news to the latest fan theories. Most-played games range from Clair Obscur to Civ to Elden Ring to Halo 2 and beyond.

Isaac Asimov was one of the most eclectic science fiction writers of all time, and while many readers know his most iconic works, such as Foundation, Galactic Empire, Bicentennial Man, I, Robot, etc., the author had a massive collection of stories that have gone largely overlooked due to the success of his most popular releases.

Throughout his prolific career, Asimov ventured far beyond the robots and sprawling future histories that have become extremely popular after the recent Apple TV Foundation series, experimenting with elaborate mysteries, social satire, and everything in between. Many of these stories originally appeared in science fiction magazines before being collected in anthologies that never got quite the same level of attention as his landmark novels.

However, some of Asimov's most inventive concepts and memorable endings are buried in the forgotten corners of his bibliography. For readers who think they've already experienced the author's best work, these five overlooked gems prove just how far ahead of his time Asimov truly was, and they're well worth tracking down.

Good Taste (1976)

Originally published in 1976 as a limited-edition standalone release from Apocalypse Press, "Good Taste" is one of Asimov's more unusual science fiction stories, exploring humanity's relationship with food in a distant, Earth-based future.

The story follows Chawker Minor, a young man returning to his home on Gammer, an artificial habitat near the Moon, after traveling to Earth and other nearby space colonies. Gammer's residents specialize in sophisticated, artificially engineered food flavors, looking down on naturally grown ingredients as primitive. However, Chawker decides to challenge these conventions by entering a prestigious culinary competition with a revolutionary new idea and a "secret" ingredient (spoiler alert: it's just garlic).

You can read "Good Taste" in The Winds of Change ... And Other Stories, found here.

Interestingly, "Good Taste" also predates several important ideas in Asimov's wider science fiction universe. Gammer's isolated society looks strangely similar to the Earth-averse Spacer civilizations explored in his Robot series, while Nemesis similarly explores humanity's early space colonies. More significantly, the story introduces the engineered food fans will recognize from Mycogen, a district of Trantor introduced in Prelude to Foundation.

Descended from ancient Spacers, Mycogen's inhabitants specialize in producing valuable microfoods, making this technology central to their economy and culture. This connection even extends to Apple TV's Foundation, with Season 3 explicitly referencing Mycogen's production of algae, fungi, spores, yeast, etc.

Each An Explorer (1956)

Originally published in the August 1956 issue of Future Science Fiction, "Each an Explorer" follows two interstellar explorers, Chouns and Smith, who discover a primitive alien civilization (or so it seems) that ends up possessing surprisingly advanced technology. Their investigation leads them to another nearby planet, where they encounter an equally mysterious society and begin questioning how these supposedly underdeveloped species got their hands on such sophisticated technologies.

Their somewhat mundane adventure turns into something far more sinister, culminating in a disturbing revelation about the true intelligence controlling these alien worlds. One of Asimov's most inventive stories focused on alien life, "Each an Explorer" is an early hidden gem that longtime readers will love.

You can read "Each an Explorer" in Buy Jupiter and Other Stories, found here.

The story was later released in Buy Jupiter and Other Stories (1975) as well as the larger collection of Asimov's work released in the 90s, the popular The Complete Stories, in the second volume. It's one of the more obscure pieces from his long career, offering a uniquely unsettling take on extraterrestrial life at a time when alien encounters and invasions had already become staples of science fiction.

Obituary (1959)

One of Asimov's more unusual science fiction mysteries, "Obituary" was originally published in the August 1959 issue of The Magazine of Fantasy and Science Fiction. The story follows Lancelot Stebbins, a brilliant but deeply resentful physicist who becomes obsessed with achieving the recognition he believes he deserves. After developing a novel method of manipulating time, Stebbins devises an elaborate scheme to fake his own death, allowing him to experience what happens in the aftermath of his passing, including his closest friends, family, and most notably, his wife's reactions.

Interestingly, the story has a somewhat tragic and personal origin, where, after reading an obituary for his friend and fellow science fiction writer Cyril M. Kornbluth in The New York Times, Asimov admitted feeling envious of the attention Kornbluth received. He realized he would never know what people would say about him after his death, and nine months later, he filtered his feelings into "Obituary" (though I don't think he had much to worry about given his legacy as one of the greatest sci-fi authors of all time).

You can read "Obituary" in Asimov's Mysteries, found here.

Beyond its fascinating origins, the story is also notable for its unusual narrative perspective. Asimov later explained in his autobiography that it was the only story he had written from a female narrator's POV, with the events recounted by Stebbins' increasingly unhappy wife. Combining dark humor, speculative sci-fi, and an ingenious mystery plot, "Obituary" showcases a very different side of Asimov's storytelling.

No Connection (1948)

Written in May 1947 and first published in the June 1948 issue of Astounding Science Fiction, "No Connection" came out at an interesting point in Isaac Asimov's early career. He had already established himself through the serialized Foundation stories and his pioneering work on the Robot series, although neither had yet been published as full books yet. "No Connection" was actually his first story unrelated to either series in more than two years at the time it came out.

Set roughly ten million years after humanity's extinction, the story imagines an Earth where intelligent bears have inherited the planet. These descendants, known as "Gurrow sapiens," inhabit North America and have developed a largely peaceful, cooperative civilization, sharing resources and advancing technologically.

You can read "No Connection" in The Early Asimov (Book 1), found here.

Readers follow Raph, a Gurrow archaeologist investigating evidence of an ancient, extinct species he calls "Primate Primeval" (aka humans). His discoveries become increasingly troubling when another intelligent race, apparently descended from chimpanzees, arrives from across the ocean. Unlike the Gurrows, these newcomers possess advanced military technology and are decidely more hostile.

As Raph investigates the remnants of Earth's forgotten civilization, he begins to suspect that the original primates, humanity, may have destroyed themselves through nuclear warfare, though Asimov keeps this ambiguous and even raises the disturbing possibility that history could repeat itself.

The Winnowing (1976)

Arguably one of the most underrated Asimov stories ever written, "The Winnowing" was originally published in the February 1976 issue of Analog Science Fiction/Science Fact, before appearing in Asimov's own The Bicentennial Man and Other Stories later that year. Unfortunately, it was largely overshadowed by the collection's titular story, which would go on to win both Hugo and Nebula Awards.

Set in a dystopian version of 2005, "The Winnowing" imagines a world devastated by overpopulation and widespread famine. Desperate to prevent humanity's collapse, the World Food Organization devises a horrifying solution: secretly introducing deadly biological agents into food supplies, potentially eliminating billions of people. When biochemist Aaron Rodman refuses to cooperate, officials threaten his family to force him to comply.

You can read "The Winnowing" in The Bicentennial Man and Other Stories, found here.

Beyond its disturbing premise, "The Winnowing" is a poignant examination of the dark implications of population-control policies and environmental extremism. Written during an era when fears of overpopulation were widespread, the story challenges the idea that humanity's survival can justify the death of thousands.

The story is still relevant in modern environmental-policy debates, including those surrounding international climate summits like COP, particularly concerning who determines which sacrifices are necessary and who must bear the consequences. However, it's worth noting that Asimov's fictional program of mass extermination is fundamentally different from the climate policies negotiated at these conferences.

Ultimately, "The Winnowing" stands out for its willingness to confront the uncomfortable moral consequences of supposedly rational solutions, culminating in one of Asimov's most unsettling endings and a prime example of one of his stories that even longtime fans probably haven't read.

While Isaac Asimov's Foundation trilogy has been a beloved sci-fi epic for decades now, the Apple TV series has introduced the story to an entirely new generation of fans who might otherwise never have discovered it. It's not surprising that longtime readers had their doubts about the adaptation, given that Asimov's original Foundation trilogy spans centuries and doesn't really focus on a single central character, instead taking a "whole is greater than the sum of its parts" approach to the narrative.

items.author: Sam Barsanti

items.text:
In the classic Ship Of Theseus thought experiment, we are meant to wonder whether or not a thing is still the thing if every piece of it has been replaced—a paradox famously presented by the regular Vision (who, of course, was just a magical recreation of the original Vision) to the sleek new White Vision (who had been reconstructed from the remains of the original Vision) near the end of WandaVision. VisionQuest seems to offer an answer to the conundrum: The Ship Of Theseus is no longer The Ship Of Theseus if it doesn’t retain The Ship Of Theseus’ memories. It’s just a Ship Of Theseus.


The new White Vision is the Vision, since he retains all of the physical pieces that made the Vision the Vision. But without having actually known Wanda or his friends in The Avengers, he’s also not the Vision. White Vision’s attempt to reconcile the differences between himself and the “real” synthezoid seems to be the guiding premise of VisionQuest, at least in its first two episodes, the second of which is actually titled “Theseus” and both reintroduces and reinterprets that aforementioned thought experiment from the perspective of a certain evil robot that lives in Vision’s attic.


But before we get to all of that, VisionQuest establishes the new status quo for White Vision—who, for the purposes of these recaps, we’re just going to start calling “Vision.” After the sitcom horrors that happened in Westview in WandaVision, Vision has moved to Edinburgh and is working in a pub that he (or, you know, the original he) and Wanda frequented when they were on the run post-Captain America: Civil War. He’s trying to revisit the life experiences the original Vision had in hopes of developing the kind of emotional connection to humans that made the original Vision a superhero.


When he’s not turning down dinner invitations from his cartoonish Irish bartender boss, he’s sitting motionless in the walk-in freezer and living in a virtual reality he built in his head. That reality takes the form of a wacky house that Vis shares with the other AI characters that Tony Stark developed in previous Marvel movies: D.U.M.-E and U from Iron Man (the silly garage robots), the original J.A.R.V.I.S. AI (played by James D’Arcy, who played the human Jarvis in Agent Carter and Avengers: Endgame), F.R.I.D.A.Y. (the AI voice that replaced J.A.R.V.I.S., played now by Orla Brady, replacing Kerry Condon when she was just a voice), and E.D.I.T.H. (the AI voice from the glasses that Stark gave to Peter Parker in Spider-Man: Far From Home, now played by Emily Hampshire instead of Dawn Michelle King).


Vis has copied their AIs and stored them in his head to both keep them alive and to utilize their various areas of expertise (J.A.R.V.I.S. is uptight but helpful, E.D.I.T.H. is wacky and likes action, and F.R.I.D.A.Y. is… Irish?), but up in the house’s attic he has imprisoned the AI mind of Ultron (played by James Spader in both his robot form and the human guise that Vis insists on everyone using). The big AI house is a fun conceit, and it’s a nice nod to the “this is all a TV show” artificiality from WandaVision and (to a lesser extent) Agatha All Along, but it’s also not always as fun as it could be or should be when Ultron’s not onscreen. Other than Vision, maybe, Ultron is the only one of the AIs that actually feels like a character and not just character traits in a human-shaped body, which may have something to do with the fact that most of the people in this wacky house are best known as disembodied voices that say stuff like “Pepper Potts is calling for you, Mr. Stark.” And they aren’t especially fleshed out beyond that, other than literally.


Thankfully, VisionQuest is not a sitcom about robots living in a virtual house, because it’s not funny enough to justify that. This is definitely more of an action show, as evidenced by the fact that Vis’ boring human coworker is almost immediately murdered by a sniper when mysterious soldiers attack the bar in hopes of capturing him. The voices in Vis’ head convince him to run away, which he does, and then we meet the leader of the mercenaries: A guy called Paladin, played by Todd Stashwick, who also has a voice in his head who’s also not as funny as the show seems to think. This one is a human, as far as we know, and she’s played by the generally very funny Diane Morgan. She’s not doing anything wrong here, but the way she just reacts to things happening on a computer doesn’t feel all that different from what you normally get out of J.A.R.V.I.S. or F.R.I.D.A.Y. It just feels like someone could’ve said “this show needs more jokes” and brought in Diane Morgan without changing a single other thing about it.


Back in his head-house, Vis finds out that Ultron has been sending messages out into the world and that he tipped off Paladin to Vision’s location. There is apparently a gigantic bounty on Vis’ head, though we don’t know who placed it yet, and Ultron was hoping that sending Paladin after him would spur Vision into doing something other than just hiding and wasting his chance to have a life.


Meanwhile, Paladin does some research into this Vision guy he’s been hired to kill, and he finds out about the Westview incident (which had been covered up by the government) and the fact that Vision had two sons in the fake reality that Wanda created. With some simple Googling, apparently, Paladin discovers police interview footage of a young man named Thomas Shepherd who, after nearly drowning in a pool (see: Agatha All Along) believes that he now has memories of two different lives in his head. In one, he’s nobody particularly special. In the other, he’s Tommy Maximoff, the son of a witch and a robot. Also more easily than you’d think, Paladin finds and kidnaps Thomas and then broadcasts a digital signal that only Vision can detect in which he says he has Vision’s son.


The second episode introduces Thomas’ backstory, or at least the relevant bit, which is that the British police decided to send him to some kind of hospital/prison after he started freaking out about having two lives in his head. While on the bus to Hospital Prison, he meets and befriends a girl named Lisa who is able to get through to him in the middle of a breakdown. She’s being sent to Hospital Prison because she’s a notorious pickpocket, which makes no sense, but she and Thomas decide to escape after she sees him accidentally use his nascent superpowers—which, at this point, just involve his hands shaking so fast that he makes electricity or rattles doors off their hinges.


Let’s not bother pretending we don’t know what’s happening here: In the comics, Tommy Maximoff is also known as Speed, a Young Avenger with super-speed powers (taking after his uncle). He is… let’s say less consequential than his brother Billy, a.k.a. Wiccan, who is married to the leader of the Kree-Skrull Empire these days. Compare that to comic book Tommy, who sometimes gets mentioned. We’re obviously heading toward this version of Tommy (who prefers Thomas) further developing super-speed powers over the course of VisionQuest, much like how Billy expanded his magical talents during Agatha All Along.


Back to the kidnapping plot: Vis doesn’t want to accept that he has a son, believing that Billy and Tommy were erased from reality when Wanda’s spell ended (if she had known that wasn’t the case, Doctor Strange In The Multiverse Of Madness would’ve been a much shorter movie). After an initial encounter with Paladin back at the bar, Vis talks to Ultron about how he doesn’t know if he should care about this kid who might be kind of the son of the other Vision. That’s when Ultron presents his own take on The Ship Of Theseus: It’s not about the ship at all, it’s about Theseus himself—the Athenian king who killed the minotaur and saved the children of Athens. Ultron says he should stop worrying about whether he’s the same as the original Vision: “When a monster has your son, don’t be the ship. Be the goddamn king.” Good line, and Spader sells it like the pro he is.


Emboldened, Vision responds to Paladin’s threat and flies off to Hospital Prison, where Thomas has been taken prisoner. After casually strolling into the lobby, he drops his own good line: “My name’s Vision and I’m here for the trap.” The staff of Hospital Prison have been replaced by Paladin’s soldiers, and they all get turned into bloody mist by Vision’s head-laser. Vis quickly finds Thomas and walks into the real trap: A magnet room that overloads his processors and threatens to destroy his electronic mind. Paladin comes in with a shotgun that fires adamantium rounds (you know all about adamantium in the MCU if you saw Captain America: Brave New World, which you probably didn’t). This basically straight-up kills Vision, which, again, seems like it was pretty easy, but he and Thomas are able to get outside and lose Paladin’s soldiers. Vision, about to die, tells Thomas to leave without him and plays up the “I don’t have feelings, I’m a robot” thing even though nobody buys it.


In Vis’ head-house, the AIs are freaking out about the fact that they’ll all die if Vis dies, so Ultron suggests that one of them makes a heroic sacrifice to free up enough processing power to save the others. J.A.R.V.I.S. decides to delete himself, reminding the others (including Ultron and Vis) that “family is forever, and it’s worth the fight.” With Vis and the AIs saved, Thomas drags Vis into a car and they drive off. Vis groans that Thomas didn’t listen to his command to save himself, to which Ultron replies, “like father, like son.”


Stray observations

• Hello True Believers, I’m Sam Barsanti and I’ll be carrying us all through the next few weeks of VisionQuest recaps. Disney+ is apparently releasing the first six two-at-a-time, so we’ll hopefully have some meaty stuff to discuss.


• Since VisionQuest is the conclusion of a trilogy of MCU TV shows, here are my thoughts on the other two: I thought WandaVision was a lot of fun, even if the Dragon Ball Z fight that ended it all was a snooze. I wasn’t overly enamored with Agatha All Along from episode to episode, but I really liked the finale and the ultimate “Witches’ Road” reveal. I do hope Agatha and Billy show up here at some point.


• As far as Marvel characters go, it would be generous to call Paladin a D-lister. Still, it’s nice that it’s a name from the comics, considering that every single other Marvel mercenary (Crossbones, Taskmaster, Bullseye, etc.) is either too famous to be included in something like this or has already appeared in the MCU.


• It seems like a waste of James D’Arcy to kill him so early, especially since now we’re left with AIs who have been recast and AIs who don’t speak. He was the guy we knew from other things!


• Every time Ultron dips into a monologue in which he makes sweeping generalizations about mankind, it might as well be Robert California insisting that “there is only sex” to Toby Flenderson. (This will likely come up again, but I love Robert California and season eight of The Office is good.)


• Other than Ultron, I’m concerned that I’ll get sick of the other AI characters and how simplistic they are. That means Thomas, as the lone human character, is going to have to carry a lot of emotional weight. We’ll see if he’s up for it.


• Before Vis goes to save Thomas, J.A.R.V.I.S. mentions that emotions can be dangerous, a fact that “he” knew better than the other AIs. The camera then holds on a painting of a figure on fire, the “he” in question, who Vis refers to as “the first of us.” Just for fun, let’s not spoil who this is referring to yet.


• VisionQuest showrunner Terry Matalas explained a while back that there would be no generative AI use in the show. That’s great, because generative AI is evil and fascist, and using it for a show about AIs would’ve at least been a slightly less desperate and insulting idea than the lazy justification behind the AI opening credits of Marvel’s Secret Invasion. I, of course, have nothing to say about that, so let’s never bring it up again.


• Seriously, though: Where are we putting Ship Of Theseus on an overplayed thought experiment tier list? Higher or lower than the Trolley Problem?

“No Strings” grade: C+

“Theseus” grade: B

Vision, about to die, tells Thomas to leave without him and plays up the “I don’t have feelings, I’m a robot” thing even though nobody buys it.

In Vis’ head-house, the AIs are freaking out about the fact that they’ll all die if Vis dies, so Ultron suggests that one of them makes a heroic sacrifice to free up enough processing power to save the others. J.A.R.V.I.S. decides to delete himself, reminding the others (including Ultron and Vis) that “family is forever, and it’s worth the fight.” With Vis and the AIs saved, Thomas drags Vis into a car and they drive off. Vis groans that Thomas didn’t listen to his command to save himself, to which Ultron replies, “like father, like son.”
Stray observations

• Hello True Believers, I’m Sam Barsanti and I’ll be carrying us all through the next few weeks of VisionQuest recaps. Disney+ is apparently releasing the first six two-at-a-time, so we’ll hopefully have some meaty stuff to discuss.

• Since VisionQuest is the conclusion of a trilogy of MCU TV shows, here are my thoughts on the other two: I thought WandaVision was a lot of fun, even if the Dragon Ball Z fight that ended it all was a snooze. I wasn’t overly enamored with Agatha All Along from episode to episode, but I really liked the finale and the ultimate “Witches’ Road” reveal. I do hope Agatha and Billy show up here at some point.

• As far as Marvel characters go, it would be generous to call Paladin a D-lister. Still, it’s nice that it’s a name from the comics, considering that every single other Marvel mercenary (Crossbones, Taskmaster, Bullseye, etc.) is either too famous to be included in something like this or has already appeared in the MCU.
• It seems like a waste of James D’Arcy to kill him so early, especially since now we’re left with AIs who have been recast and AIs who don’t speak. He was the guy we knew from other things!

• Every time Ultron dips into a monologue in which he makes sweeping generalizations about mankind, it might as well be Robert California insisting that “there is only sex” to Toby Flenderson. (This will likely come up again, but I love Robert California and season eight of The Office is good.)

• Other than Ultron, I’m concerned that I’ll get sick of the other AI characters and how simplistic they are. That means Thomas, as the lone human character, is going to have to carry a lot of emotional weight. We’ll see if he’s up for it.

• Before Vis goes to save Thomas, J.A.R.V.I.S. mentions that emotions can be dangerous, a fact that “he” knew better than the other AIs. The camera then holds on a painting of a figure on fire, the “he” in question, who Vis refers to as “the first of us.” Just for fun, let’s not spoil who this is referring to yet.

• VisionQuest showrunner Terry Matalas explained a while back that there would be no generative AI use in the show. That’s great, because generative AI is evil and fascist, and using it for a show about AIs would’ve at least been a slightly less desperate and insulting idea than the lazy justification behind the AI opening credits of Marvel’s Secret Invasion. I, of course, have nothing to say about that, so let’s never bring it up again.
• Seriously, though: Where are we putting Ship Of Theseus on an overplayed thought experiment tier list? Higher or lower than the Trolley Problem?
“No Strings” grade: C+
“Theseus” grade: B

items.text:
The first thing I noticed when waking up in the city of Nivalis for the first time is that it’s gorgeous. My top-floor apartment there overlooks a neon-illuminated cyberpunk metropolis, and the way the rain inches down my windows and reflects the neon’s multicolored glow just looks stunning. I quickly learned that things aren’t as charming outside, though—there’s a killer on the loose, a malicious megacorp controlling everything, a mandatory curfew enforced by security bots, the looming burden of debt, and, best of all, an NPC who threatened to give me the recipe for “Go Fuck Yourself Pie.”

I was immediately excited by all of this when I launched Nivalis Nights, a cyberpunk restaurant management and life sim that’s also ION LANDS’ follow-up to Cloudpunk. I put a few hours into it this week, and I was really looking forward to finally playing a management sim with a grittier edge. Unfortunately, its ambition feels awkwardly compressed, leading to a game whose first few hours have felt incredibly overwhelming and a tad undercooked.

The second thing I noticed after I woke up was Ava, who quickly became my nemesis. Ava is an automaton who lacks a physical presence and is instead apparently baked into my brain, existing somewhere in there in order to deliver tutorials and chat with me. (I honestly forgot how she explained her own existence. That’s because I didn’t want to listen to her at all!)

The problem with Ava being basically part of me is that she interrupts everything. Instead of being an NPC who texts me on an in-game phone or even just telepathically communicates via little popups, Ava’s dialogue takes over my entire screen at random, blocking me from movement until she’s done talking to me. It’s pretty jarring to be walking to the market, intent on restocking my restaurant’s ingredients, only to be stopped dead in my tracks without warning by Ava again.

That being said, I’m a little glad that Ava only exists in my brain because I just can’t get myself to jive with this game’s character models. Despite almost everything else in the world of Nivalis being impressively built out of voxels, its characters (and their outfits, some of which seem deeply uncool) are 3D modeled in a Fortnite-y style that’s not nearly as stylish as the world that surrounds them. Like, here’s Nivalis:

And then here’s just Some Guy:

These character models matter a lot more than expected, too. Despite mostly being marketed as a restaurant sim, so far Nivalis Nights has turned out to be more of a visual novel packed with fetch quests, so you’re staring at these characters a lot. There is a romance system here, but I…think I’ll stay single for a while. It’s a shame that I feel this way about these characters because their pixel art portraits, which pop up occasionally but not nearly enough, are excellent!

Thankfully, the restaurant management part of Nivalis is nice. I was shocked by just how many ingredients are available, and there are an adequate number of recipes to throw them into, too. However, I found myself missing a few mechanics that seem like staples in most modern restaurant sims. Dave the Diver and KuloNiku: Bowl Up! keeps things exciting with lots of minigames, for example—meanwhile, Nivalis just makes me stare at the same food processor animation over and over and over again whenever I jump in to help my employees out.

I still enjoyed the restaurant grind, though, and it felt especially rewarding to unlock new recipes and upgrades as I progressed. But just as soon as I had begun getting into the groove of running my own restaurant, my assistant let me know that it was time to purchase a second one. I was genuinely shocked—my first restaurant was barely even turning a profit yet, my customers were still rating their meals three stars, I literally owned two tables, and not even three full in-game days had passed yet! The main story of Nivalis, which players have said is about 20 hours long, boasts 14 businesses to own, so I can’t imagine that players might get any time to settle into the rest of these other locales, either.

The rest of my time with Nivalis felt equally unfocused. I was constantly whisked away into new quests despite already being in the middle of several others, which left me with an ever-expanding, unorganizable quest log that devoured a chunk of my HUD. Almost immediately after I unlocked the greenhouse, I unlocked a boat, which seem like two pretty major features that should be given a bit of time to marinate. Instead, they both went by so quickly that I never even had a chance to be excited about these new unlocks. I felt like a kid shredding open all of their gifts at once on Christmas morning, giving so little thought to each one that they finish and then say, “that’s it?”

Nivalis Nights clearly has some good bones: it’s gorgeous, it has a really intriguing premise, a lot of the voice acting is solid, and it’s incredibly ambitious. But I couldn’t help but feel like the devs could have given this one a bit more time in the oven food processor, mostly to adjust the game’s breakneck pacing and let its ideas simmer for a bit (or just chop some entirely).

While writing this, I haven’t been able to stop thinking about how one of my restaurant’s first customers in Nivalis Nights walked in with a chunky mask on and proceeded to sit down, order food, and attempt to eat it, all without removing the mask. It was just a slightly silly animation oversight, but I also felt exactly like him while playing through the game’s first few hours. Really, we were in the same boat: I’m sure there was a good meal in front of me, but I never got the chance to taste it.

items.title: What to watch on Peacock: The best shows streaming right now
items.author: The A.V. Club
items.summary: Peacock is one of the most underrated platforms of the streaming era. In addition to what is inarguably the best live sports access of any streaming service,
items.text:
Peacock is one of the most underrated platforms of the streaming era. In addition to what is inarguably the best live sports access of any streaming service, its vast library offers easy access to comfort watches and bingeable classics like 30 Rock, Parks And Recreation, and The Office. But many viewers are likely less familiar with Peacock’s slate of original programming, which comprises an intriguing array of buzzy dramas, offbeat comedies, true-crime series, and everyone’s favorite castle-set reality competition, The Traitors.


Peacock’s big hook for spooky season is its forthcoming Friday The 13th prequel series, Crystal Lake, an origin story that stars Linda Cardellini as the hockey mask-wearing Jason’s mother, Pamela Voorhees. But the streamer also boasts several other intriguingly offbeat horror offerings for those who are looking for something a bit different this month, including the Satanic Panic horror-comedy series Hysteria! and charming werewolf rom-com Wolf Like Me.


Here are more of our picks (in alphabetical order) for the Peacock series you should stream right now.


This list was updated on October 13, 2026.

All Her Fault


Stars: Sarah Snook, Jake Lacy, Dakota Fanning, Jay Ellis, Abby Elliott, Michael Peña, Thomas Cocquerel, Daniel Monks


Number of seasons: One


Sarah Snook kicked off her post-Succession career with this twisty, high-tension thriller based on the novel of the same name by Andrea Mara. Snook stars as Marissa, a mother who drops her young son off for a playdate, only to return to find that the family living in the house aren’t people she recognizes and her child is missing. As Marissa and her husband (Jake Lacy) race to find Milo, a near-constant stream of shocking secrets are revealed.

Angelyne


Stars: Emmy Rossum, Martin Freeman, Lukas Gage, Hamish Linklater, Alex Karpovsky, Molly Ephraim, Phillip Ettinger, Michael Angarano


Number of seasons: One


You’ve never seen Emmy Rossum like this before. The Shameless star transforms into the singer, actor, and media personality Angelyne, who became known throughout Los Angeles in the ’80s for her billboard advertisements. Angelyne is a five-part series exploring her rise to fame and journalist Jeff Glaser’s 2010 attempt to uncover her real-life story.

The Capture


Stars: Holliday Granger, Ron Perlman, Lia Williams, Ben Miles, Shaun Evans, Paapa Essiedu, Ginny Holder, Cavan Clerkin, Indira Varma, Daisy Waterstone


Number of seasons: Three


This almost uncomfortably timely British techno-thriller kicks off with London detective DCI Rachel Carey (Granger) tasked with investigating a crime the suspect insists he didn’t commit. So far, so seen it in the world of procedurals, except this time, there’s a frightening twist. The accused is innocent, and someone’s made a deepfake so convincing that an innocent man almost went to jail. As the series continues, other technological nightmares crop up, and it becomes increasingly clear that the truth isn’t as important as what you can convince people to believe.

The Day Of The Jackal


Stars: Eddie Redmayne, Lashana Lynch, Úrsula Corberó, Chukwudi Iwuji, Lia Williams, Charles Dance, Richard Dormer, Khalid Abdalla, Eleanor Matsurra


Number of seasons: One


This modern-day spin on the classic 1971 spy novel of the same name stars Eddie Redmayne as the titular Jackal, the elusive assassin known for his high-profile kills. But when one near-impossible kill shot catches the attention of tenacious MI6 agent Bianca (Lynch), a cat and mouse chase for the ages begins. Redmayne is fantastic as the chameleon-like killer for hire, who loves elaborate disguises, fake accents and high-tech weaponry as much as any iteration of Bond. The series has been renewed for a second season.

Devil In Disguise: John Wayne Gacy


Stars: Michael Chernus, Marin Ireland, Gabriel Luna, Michael Angarano, James Badge Dale, Chris Sullivan


Number of seasons: One


Based on Peacock’s own 2021 docuseries John Wayne Gacy: Devil in Disguise (no title confusion there!), this scripted true-crime series is a breath of fresh air in a landscape that tends to skew more heavily toward the lurid and sensational. With a focus on the stories of the victims and their families, the series manages to tell the story of Gacy’s horrific crimes—he killed dozens of men and boys in the 1970s—without glamorizing the man who committed them.

Everything I Know About Love


Stars: Emma Appleton, Bel Powley, Marli Siu, Aliyah Odoffin, Connor Finch, Baxter Ryan Bown, Jordan Peters, Juliet Cowan, Alexander Lincoln, Jill Halfpenny, Craig Parkinson


Number of seasons: One


Adapted from her own bestselling memoir, Dolly Alderton’s love letter to female friendship and the chaotic messiness of love and life in your twenties is delightful from start to finish. The series follows four young women who share a London house together as they engage in some lighthearted early 2010s-style debauchery, make poor decisions, struggle with post-college poverty, and show up for one another when they need it. Breezy and warm, Everything I Know About Love features its fair share of relationship disasters, but its best love story is between the friends at its center.

A Friend Of The Family


Stars: Jake Lacy, Anna Paquin, Colin Hanks, Lio Tipton, Hendrix Yancey, McKenna Grace, Austin Stowell, Patrick Fischler, Philip Ettinger


Number of seasons: One


A Friend Of The Family expands on the wild real-life story explored in the 2019 documentary Abducted In Plain Sight. In excruciating but well-plotted detail, the drama unpacks how a teenage Jan Broberg was kidnapped twice in the ’70s by a predatory friend of the family who was obsessed with her.

The Five Star Weekend


Stars: Jennifer Garner, Chloë Sevigny, Regina Hall, D’Arcy Carden, Gemma Chan, Harlow Jane, Timothy Olyphant, Judy Greer, David Denman


Number of seasons: One


Based on a novel by beach read queen Elin Hilderbrand, The Five Star Weekend follows a grieving food influencer (Garner) who hosts a luxurious girls weekend on Nantucket in the wake of her husband’s death with four of her closest friends, each of whom is going through her own personal and emotional upheavals. An ode to female friendship and the glorious vistas of the New England coast, it’s a cozy watch with just enough melodrama to keep things interesting throughout. It’s been renewed for a second season.

Killing It


Stars: Craig Robinson, Claudia O’Doherty, Scott MacArthur, Stephanie Nogueras, Tim Heidecker, Zach Grenier


Number of seasons: Two


This enjoyable, irreverent comedy centers on Craig, a divorced single father who fails to secure a loan for his new business. However, he learns from his Australian Uber driver, Jillian, that there’s a lot of money to be made by hunting snakes. So they both participate in the South Florida Python Challenge for a $20,000 prize, showcasing a funny dynamic along the way. In season two, they finally start their farm—only to be met with a barrage of new challenges.

Lockerbie: A Search For Truth


Stars: Colin Firth, Catherine McCormack, Sam Troughton, Ardalan Esmaili, Mark Bonnar, Jemma Carlton


Number of seasons: One


This true-crime saga is based on the 1988 Lockerbie plane bombing that killed 270 people—Firth plays Dr. Jim Swire, whose daughter was a victim in the incident. Her death puts him on an unfathomable mission to unmask the terrorists, even if it means traveling to the Middle East, the Netherlands, and elsewhere (and standing up to various political leaders) to do so.

Long Bright River


Stars: Amanda Seyfried, Britne Olford, Ashleigh Cummings, John Doman, Nicholas Pinnock, Callum Vinson


Number of seasons: One


Amanda Seyfried shines in this Mare Of Easttown-style limited series as a Philadelphia patrol officer who investigates the murders of three women that she hopes tie into the disappearance of her sister. Adapted from Liz Moore’s novel, the story also explores systemic issues of drug addiction and poverty that allow so many of our country’s most vulnerable to fall through the cracks.

Mrs. Davis


Stars: Betty Gilpin, Jake McDorman, Margo Martindale, Elizabeth Marvel, Andy McQueen, Tom Wlaschiha, Katja Herbers, Chris Diamantopoulos


Number of seasons: One


Damon Lindelof and Tara Hernandez’s Mrs. Davis is nothing if not unexpected (read: brace yourself for plenty of exciting twists). In the timely sci-fi dramedy, a novice nun teams up with her ex-boyfriend in a battle against AI that takes them on a globe-spanning journey. Mrs. Davis is an unpredictable ride that ends with a satisfying conclusion.

The Paper


Stars: Domhnall Gleeson, Chelsea Frei, Sabrina Impacciatore, Melvin Gregg, Ramona Young, Oscar Nuñez, Alex Edelstein


Number of seasons: One


Greg Daniels teams up with Nathan For You’s Michael Koman for this spin-off of The Office, in which the camera crew that followed Dunder Mifflin’s employees chronicles the kooky volunteers at an Ohio newspaper, the Toledo Truth Teller. Gleeson plays Ned, the Truth Teller’s new editor-in-chief, a former toilet paper salesman with a journalism degree who wants to return the paper to its glory days as a trusted community resource. (The dream!) Hijinks predictably ensue, but The Paper is altogether kinder and warmer than its Scranton-based predecessor. Season two premieres in September.

Poker Face


Stars: Natasha Lyonne, Benjamin Bratt, Simon Helberg, Rhea Perlman, John Mulaney, Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Simon Rex, Patti Harrison


Number of seasons: Two


Natasha Lyonne leads Rian Johnson’s delightful case-of-the-week show as Charlie Cale, who goes on the run when her wealthy casino boss seeks revenge on her. With an uncanny ability to detect lies, she hops from city to city to solve murders (and deals with some fantastic and fun guest stars). And despite its cancellation last year, Johnson hopes to make a third season led by Peter Dinklage.

PONIES


Stars: Emilia Clarke, Hayley Lu Richardson, Adrian Lester, Artjom Gilz, Vic Michaelis, Nicholas Podany, Petro Ninovskyi


Number of seasons: One


The unfortunately named PONIES is almost certainly one of the best shows on this streamer that almost no one has heard about. Named after a military acronym for Persons of No Interest—a.k.a. the everyday people who fly under the radar and are of no interest to foreign powers—the 1970s-set series follows a pair of widowed secretaries at the American embassy in Moscow who become spies after their husbands die in mysterious circumstances. Clarke and Richardson have outstanding chemistry together, and the show’s brisk pace makes it an easy binge.

The Resort


Stars: Cristin Milioti, William Jackson Harper, Luis Gerardo Méndez, Skyler Gisondo, Nina Bloomgarden, Gabriela Cartol, Nick Offerman


Number of seasons: One


A surprisingly inventive offbeat comedy-thriller about a married couple who book a vacation at a lush holiday resort for their 10th anniversary only to find themselves pulled into an unsolved mystery about two missing persons from 15 years earlier. The show’s The White Lotus meets Indiana Jones vibes are unique on this—or likely any other—platform, and Harper and Miloti are a dream together.

Rutherford Falls


Stars: Ed Helms, Jana Schmieding, Michael Greyeyes, Dustin Milligan, Jesse Leigh, Beth Stelling, Bobby Wilson, Devery Jacobs, Dana L. Wilson


Number of seasons: Two


Peacock executives didn’t know how good they had it with Rutherford Falls. Even though the comedy was canceled after two seasons, it remains one of their top-tier originals. Co-created by Sierra Teller Ornelas, Mike Schur, and series star Ed Helms, it centers on childhood best friends Nathan and Reagan, who find themselves at a crossroads when a crisis hits their small town. Moreover, the show is a joyful exploration of the Indigenous community, with scene-stealing performances from Greyeyes and Schmieding.


The Traitors


Stars: Alan Cumming


Number of seasons: Four


Hosted by Alan Cumming, this reality show sees 20 contestants face off in a castle in the Scottish Highlands in the hopes of winning a $250,000 prize. Among the “Faithful” players are some “Traitors”—that is, people selected by the host whose goal is to eliminate the rest and claim the cash for themselves. It’s a great time, and Cumming is as charming as ever. The series has been renewed through seasons 5 and 6, and an all-civilian version, The Traitors: New Blood, premieres in September.

We Are Lady Parts


Stars: Anjana Vasan, Sarah Kameela Impey, Faith Omole, Lucie Shorthouse, Juliette Motamed, Aiysha Hart, Shobu Kapoor, Zaqi Ismail


Number of seasons: Two


Nida Manzoor’s unique comedy centers on the eponymous all-female Muslim punk band looking to make a name for themselves in the male-dominated U.K. music scene. A joyful, feminist mix of culture clash humor and heartfelt friendship, the briskly paced series, quite literally, rocks. (Plus, the original songs are so damn catchy you won’t be able to get them out of your head.


Vigil


Stars: Suranne Jones, Rose Leslie, Gary Lewis, Orla Russell


Number of seasons: Two


An exceptional British procedural thriller that sees Suranne Jones solving crimes in a series of unique and high-stakes locations alongside an assortment of high-profile guest stars, Vigil is a great example of the sort of underrated (and underpromoted) British TV regularly available on Peacock. The series’ first season involves a mysterious death on a British nuclear submarine, while its second centers on a compromised Royal Air Force drone that kills several soldiers. A third season, set in the Arctic, is coming soon.

Peacock’s big hook for spooky season is its forthcoming Friday The 13th prequel series, Crystal Lake, an origin story that stars Linda Cardellini as the hockey mask-wearing Jason’s mother, Pamela Voorhees. But the streamer also boasts several other intriguingly offbeat horror offerings for those who are looking for something a bit different this month, including the Satanic Panic horror-comedy series Hysteria! and charming werewolf rom-com Wolf Like Me.
Here are more of our picks (in alphabetical order) for the Peacock series you should stream right now.
This list was updated on October 13, 2026.
All Her Fault
Stars: Sarah Snook, Jake Lacy, Dakota Fanning, Jay Ellis, Abby Elliott, Michael Peña, Thomas Cocquerel, Daniel Monks
Number of seasons: One

Sarah Snook kicked off her post-Succession career with this twisty, high-tension thriller based on the novel of the same name by Andrea Mara. Snook stars as Marissa, a mother who drops her young son off for a playdate, only to return to find that the family living in the house aren’t people she recognizes and her child is missing. As Marissa and her husband (Jake Lacy) race to find Milo, a near-constant stream of shocking secrets are revealed.
Angelyne
Stars: Emmy Rossum, Martin Freeman, Lukas Gage, Hamish Linklater, Alex Karpovsky, Molly Ephraim, Phillip Ettinger, Michael Angarano
Number of seasons: One

You’ve never seen Emmy Rossum like this before. The Shameless star transforms into the singer, actor, and media personality Angelyne, who became known throughout Los Angeles in the ’80s for her billboard advertisements. Angelyne is a five-part series exploring her rise to fame and journalist Jeff Glaser’s 2010 attempt to uncover her real-life story.
The Capture
Stars: Holliday Granger, Ron Perlman, Lia Williams, Ben Miles, Shaun Evans, Paapa Essiedu, Ginny Holder, Cavan Clerkin, Indira Varma, Daisy Waterstone
Number of seasons: Three

This almost uncomfortably timely British techno-thriller kicks off with London detective DCI Rachel Carey (Granger) tasked with investigating a crime the suspect insists he didn’t commit. So far, so seen it in the world of procedurals, except this time, there’s a frightening twist. The accused is innocent, and someone’s made a deepfake so convincing that an innocent man almost went to jail. As the series continues, other technological nightmares crop up, and it becomes increasingly clear that the truth isn’t as important as what you can convince people to believe.
The Day Of The Jackal
Stars: Eddie Redmayne, Lashana Lynch, Úrsula Corberó, Chukwudi Iwuji, Lia Williams, Charles Dance, Richard Dormer, Khalid Abdalla, Eleanor Matsurra
Number of seasons: One

This modern-day spin on the classic 1971 spy novel of the same name stars Eddie Redmayne as the titular Jackal, the elusive assassin known for his high-profile kills. But when one near-impossible kill shot catches the attention of tenacious MI6 agent Bianca (Lynch), a cat and mouse chase for the ages begins. Redmayne is fantastic as the chameleon-like killer for hire, who loves elaborate disguises, fake accents and high-tech weaponry as much as any iteration of Bond. The series has been renewed for a second season.
Devil In Disguise: John Wayne Gacy
Stars: Michael Chernus, Marin Ireland, Gabriel Luna, Michael Angarano, James Badge Dale, Chris Sullivan
Number of seasons: One

Based on Peacock’s own 2021 docuseries John Wayne Gacy: Devil in Disguise (no title confusion there!), this scripted true-crime series is a breath of fresh air in a landscape that tends to skew more heavily toward the lurid and sensational. With a focus on the stories of the victims and their families, the series manages to tell the story of Gacy’s horrific crimes—he killed dozens of men and boys in the 1970s—without glamorizing the man who committed them.
Everything I Know About Love
Stars: Emma Appleton, Bel Powley, Marli Siu, Aliyah Odoffin, Connor Finch, Baxter Ryan Bown, Jordan Peters, Juliet Cowan, Alexander Lincoln, Jill Halfpenny, Craig Parkinson
Number of seasons: One

Adapted from her own bestselling memoir, Dolly Alderton’s love letter to female friendship and the chaotic messiness of love and life in your twenties is delightful from start to finish. The series follows four young women who share a London house together as they engage in some lighthearted early 2010s-style debauchery, make poor decisions, struggle with post-college poverty, and show up for one another when they need it. Breezy and warm, Everything I Know About Love features its fair share of relationship disasters, but its best love story is between the friends at its center.
A Friend Of The Family
Stars: Jake Lacy, Anna Paquin, Colin Hanks, Lio Tipton, Hendrix Yancey, McKenna Grace, Austin Stowell, Patrick Fischler, Philip Ettinger
Number of seasons: One

A Friend Of The Family expands on the wild real-life story explored in the 2019 documentary Abducted In Plain Sight. In excruciating but well-plotted detail, the drama unpacks how a teenage Jan Broberg was kidnapped twice in the ’70s by a predatory friend of the family who was obsessed with her.
The Five Star Weekend
Stars: Jennifer Garner, Chloë Sevigny, Regina Hall, D’Arcy Carden, Gemma Chan, Harlow Jane, Timothy Olyphant, Judy Greer, David Denman
Number of seasons: One

Based on a novel by beach read queen Elin Hilderbrand, The Five Star Weekend follows a grieving food influencer (Garner) who hosts a luxurious girls weekend on Nantucket in the wake of her husband’s death with four of her closest friends, each of whom is going through her own personal and emotional upheavals. An ode to female friendship and the glorious vistas of the New England coast, it’s a cozy watch with just enough melodrama to keep things interesting throughout. It’s been renewed for a second season.
Killing It
Stars: Craig Robinson, Claudia O’Doherty, Scott MacArthur, Stephanie Nogueras, Tim Heidecker, Zach Grenier
Number of seasons: Two

This enjoyable, irreverent comedy centers on Craig, a divorced single father who fails to secure a loan for his new business. However, he learns from his Australian Uber driver, Jillian, that there’s a lot of money to be made by hunting snakes. So they both participate in the South Florida Python Challenge for a $20,000 prize, showcasing a funny dynamic along the way. In season two, they finally start their farm—only to be met with a barrage of new challenges.
Lockerbie: A Search For Truth
Stars: Colin Firth, Catherine McCormack, Sam Troughton, Ardalan Esmaili, Mark Bonnar, Jemma Carlton
Number of seasons: One

This true-crime saga is based on the 1988 Lockerbie plane bombing that killed 270 people—Firth plays Dr. Jim Swire, whose daughter was a victim in the incident. Her death puts him on an unfathomable mission to unmask the terrorists, even if it means traveling to the Middle East, the Netherlands, and elsewhere (and standing up to various political leaders) to do so.
Long Bright River
Stars: Amanda Seyfried, Britne Olford, Ashleigh Cummings, John Doman, Nicholas Pinnock, Callum Vinson
Number of seasons: One

Amanda Seyfried shines in this Mare Of Easttown-style limited series as a Philadelphia patrol officer who investigates the murders of three women that she hopes tie into the disappearance of her sister. Adapted from Liz Moore’s novel, the story also explores systemic issues of drug addiction and poverty that allow so many of our country’s most vulnerable to fall through the cracks.
Mrs. Davis
Stars: Betty Gilpin, Jake McDorman, Margo Martindale, Elizabeth Marvel, Andy McQueen, Tom Wlaschiha, Katja Herbers, Chris Diamantopoulos
Number of seasons: One

Damon Lindelof and Tara Hernandez’s Mrs. Davis is nothing if not unexpected (read: brace yourself for plenty of exciting twists). In the timely sci-fi dramedy, a novice nun teams up with her ex-boyfriend in a battle against AI that takes them on a globe-spanning journey. Mrs. Davis is an unpredictable ride that ends with a satisfying conclusion.
The Paper
Stars: Domhnall Gleeson, Chelsea Frei, Sabrina Impacciatore, Melvin Gregg, Ramona Young, Oscar Nuñez, Alex Edelstein
Number of seasons: One

Greg Daniels teams up with Nathan For You’s Michael Koman for this spin-off of The Office, in which the camera crew that followed Dunder Mifflin’s employees chronicles the kooky volunteers at an Ohio newspaper, the Toledo Truth Teller. Gleeson plays Ned, the Truth Teller’s new editor-in-chief, a former toilet paper salesman with a journalism degree who wants to return the paper to its glory days as a trusted community resource. (The dream!) Hijinks predictably ensue, but The Paper is altogether kinder and warmer than its Scranton-based predecessor. Season two premieres in September.
Poker Face
Stars: Natasha Lyonne, Benjamin Bratt, Simon Helberg, Rhea Perlman, John Mulaney, Giancarlo Esposito, Cynthia Erivo, Simon Rex, Patti Harrison
Number of seasons: Two

Natasha Lyonne leads Rian Johnson’s delightful case-of-the-week show as Charlie Cale, who goes on the run when her wealthy casino boss seeks revenge on her. With an uncanny ability to detect lies, she hops from city to city to solve murders (and deals with some fantastic and fun guest stars). And despite its cancellation last year, Johnson hopes to make a third season led by Peter Dinklage.
PONIES
Stars: Emilia Clarke, Hayley Lu Richardson, Adrian Lester, Artjom Gilz, Vic Michaelis, Nicholas Podany, Petro Ninovskyi
Number of seasons: One

The unfortunately named PONIES is almost certainly one of the best shows on this streamer that almost no one has heard about. Named after a military acronym for Persons of No Interest—a.k.a. the everyday people who fly under the radar and are of no interest to foreign powers—the 1970s-set series follows a pair of widowed secretaries at the American embassy in Moscow who become spies after their husbands die in mysterious circumstances. Clarke and Richardson have outstanding chemistry together, and the show’s brisk pace makes it an easy binge.
The Resort
Stars: Cristin Milioti, William Jackson Harper, Luis Gerardo Méndez, Skyler Gisondo, Nina Bloomgarden, Gabriela Cartol, Nick Offerman
Number of seasons: One

A surprisingly inventive offbeat comedy-thriller about a married couple who book a vacation at a lush holiday resort for their 10th anniversary only to find themselves pulled into an unsolved mystery about two missing persons from 15 years earlier. The show’s The White Lotus meets Indiana Jones vibes are unique on this—or likely any other—platform, and Harper and Miloti are a dream together.
Rutherford Falls
Stars: Ed Helms, Jana Schmieding, Michael Greyeyes, Dustin Milligan, Jesse Leigh, Beth Stelling, Bobby Wilson, Devery Jacobs, Dana L. Wilson
Number of seasons: Two

Co-created by Sierra Teller Ornelas, Mike Schur, and series star Ed Helms, it centers on childhood best friends Nathan and Reagan, who find themselves at a crossroads when a crisis hits their small town. Moreover, the show is a joyful exploration of the Indigenous community, with scene-stealing performances from Greyeyes and Schmieding.
The Traitors
Stars: Alan Cumming
Number of seasons: Four

Hosted by Alan Cumming, this reality show sees 20 contestants face off in a castle in the Scottish Highlands in the hopes of winning a $250,000 prize. Among the “Faithful” players are some “Traitors”—that is, people selected by the host whose goal is to eliminate the rest and claim the cash for themselves. It’s a great time, and Cumming is as charming as ever. The series has been renewed through seasons 5 and 6, and an all-civilian version, The Traitors: New Blood, premieres in September.
We Are Lady Parts
Stars: Anjana Vasan, Sarah Kameela Impey, Faith Omole, Lucie Shorthouse, Juliette Motamed, Aiysha Hart, Shobu Kapoor, Zaqi Ismail
Number of seasons: Two

Nida Manzoor’s unique comedy centers on the eponymous all-female Muslim punk band looking to make a name for themselves in the male-dominated U.K. music scene. A joyful, feminist mix of culture clash humor and heartfelt friendship, the briskly paced series, quite literally, rocks. (Plus, the original songs are so damn catchy you won’t be able to get them out of your head.
Vigil
Stars: Suranne Jones, Rose Leslie, Gary Lewis, Orla Russell
Number of seasons: Two

An exceptional British procedural thriller that sees Suranne Jones solving crimes in a series of unique and high-stakes locations alongside an assortment of high-profile guest stars, Vigil is a great example of the sort of underrated (and underpromoted) British TV regularly available on Peacock. The series’ first season involves a mysterious death on a British nuclear submarine, while its second centers on a compromised Royal Air Force drone that kills several soldiers. A third season, set in the Arctic, is coming soon.
