items.text:
“Brilliant. And scary.”

That was my instant reply to a text from a friend the morning after we saw the world premiere of Luca Guadagnino’s “Artificial” at the New York Film Festival. The NYFF hasn’t been known for world premieres, or at least it wasn’t until last year, when A24 unveiled Josh Safdie’s “Marty Supreme” in a surprise screening event, launching it to major critical acclaim, a world box office near $200 million, and Oscar nominations, including Best Picture. That success reportedly inspired other distributors to see the festival as a place for world premieres, and it may have inspired the NYFF as well: this year it hosted seven.

As widely reported, Amazon MGM produced Guadagnino’s film, but then dropped it and Neon picked it up. Did the larger company fear Silicon Valley’s reception? While “Artificial” takes a probing approach to AI, it doesn’t come across as an indictment of the forces producing it. Rather, it is a very engaging, dramatic and sometimes quite funny portrait of a particular slice of that culture, one that developed over several years and led to a particularly notorious incident: the attempt of the board of OpenAI to oust its charismatic CEO, Sam Altman, and his fast and successful campaign to turn the tables and overthrow his opponents.

What do such boardroom machinations have to do with the promise and perils of Artificial Intelligence? Actually, “Artificial” makes a strong case that the human element, all the imponderables of personality, ego, and conflicting agendas, shapes how this technology is being ushered into the world, and what it may do to it.

The film, please note, doesn’t predict anything–neither utopia nor dystopia. Yet by focusing on the recent past rather than the impending future, it shows how AI’s rapid development has raised an accelerating set of questions and problematic possibilities.

At the Q&A following the NYFF premiere, the film’s original screenwriter, Simon Rich (former SNL writer and son of columnist Frank Rich), said he’d been concerned about AI since a childhood friend warned him of its dangers. He’s clearly studied the subject in depth, because “Artificial”‘s script brings a sense of authenticity to a complex story, even as it necessarily condenses it. That Rich’s fast-paced dialogue may sometimes overwhelm viewers with flurries of tech jargon, but it only serves the story’s immersive flow.

It begins in Toronto in 2003 when a 17-year-old native of Russia, Ilya Sutskever (Yura Borisov), enters the lab of future Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton (a terrific Mark Rylance) and so impresses the brilliant professor that a partnership is soon born, one that will take them to Silicon Valley and the hallways and workspaces of Google. A decade-plus later, their pioneering AI work attracts the interest of Stanford dropout Sam Altman (Andrew Garfield) and his pal Elon Musk (Ike Barinholtz). The charming but morally slippery Altman recognizes the genius of upright, idealistic Sutskever and offers a corporate collaboration meant to bring immeasurable benefits to the human race, while, of course, enriching the technology’s masterminds.

OpenAI was founded in 2016. The boardroom battle that forms the story’s crux comes in 2023. In the intervening years, we see the rise of a fast-paced, celebratory culture among young people, forcing a technological revolution whose nature no one understands. For viewers who’ve followed this tale in news reports and magazine articles, it’s fascinating to see how Guadagnino and Rich bring the characters, their labors and conflicts to life. But perhaps the best thing about the film is that it doesn’t require any advance knowledge of its subject and milieu; newcomers are just as likely to be swept up in its torrent of events and emotions.

This is filmmaking of a very high order. Arguably Guadagnino’s best work (it’s leagues beyond his “After the Hunt,” which opened the NYFF last year), “Artificial” has a great sense of atmosphere and a constantly evolving narrative drive. As for the acting, it might be best described as a semicircle. On one side, there’s the film’s most focused and realistic performance (and the one that will deservedly garner the most praise), Borisov’s Ilya Sutskever. On the other side, Barinholtz’s cartoonish Elon Musk is so broad it almost doesn’t work.

Between these extremes, and borrowing elements of both, Garfield’s Sam Altman is forceful but duplicitous: a gifted leader and a quasi-sociopath. As the story progresses, especially at the climactic showdown with Sutskever and OpenAI’s board, Altman’s personal power becomes increasingly crucial. He’s obviously not the only billionaire calling the shots in the AI game, but he makes you wonder: Do we really want the planet’s future in his hands?

The world premiere of “Artificial” at the NYFF felt eerily timely. Although it could not have been predicted by the filmmakers or the festival, just a month before the film’s screening, a 27-year-old AI researcher named Jacob Coxon, who had worked at OpenAI and resigned from Anthropic, issued a statement saying, “The people building AI earnestly believe that it could kill us all by the end of the decade…[M]any executives and senior researchers will couch their phrasing in the press to sound sensible—but I hear the same people express fear privately. No other human activity poses this level of danger.”

That warning has reverberated worldwide and sparked wide discussions about the dangers of AI and the need to contain it. Among other greater consequences, it might well make “Artificial” the most important dramatic movie of 2026. And while I understand Neon’s Oscar strategy of releasing the film on Christmas Day, I left its world premiere not only shaken and dazed, but also wishing it could go into theaters the next day.

Notes on some of the other world premieres at the 2026 New York Film Festival:

Mani Haghighi’s “I Deserve a Lover Whose Every Rise Sets Fiery Dooms Raging Across the Skies” is a documentary portrait of two Iranians as eccentric as the film’s title: painter and conceptual artist Nasser Bakshi and his partner Roghayeh Najdi. The duo has assembled a vast archive of artworks and found objects that chronicle the lives of ordinary Iranians across generations, and the film (shot just before the current U.S./Israel war on Iran) explores their world in an amusingly digressive, unconventional way. A leader in the post-Kiarostami generation of Iranian filmmakers, Haghighi isn’t primarily a documentarian (his masterpiece “A Dragon Arrives!” really deserves a belated U.S. release), but it’s great to see one of his films at the NYFF.

I imagine that Tony Gilroy’s “Behemoth!” will have its admirers, but I am unfortunately not one. Which is a shame: I’m a fan of Gilroy’s Jason Bourne scripts and especially his complex, brainy 2007 thriller “Michael Clayton,” which he wrote and directed. His new film starts promisingly: a professional cellist (Pedro Pascal) enters a Los Angeles recording studio to work on the score for a new movie.

Gilroy reportedly worked with nine composers to shape the drama’s musical dimension, and that element has its pleasures and fascinations. But they merely form the aural wallpaper of a hodgepodge story that jumps around in time and space, chronicling the cellist’s soap-operatic life. While Pascal, one of our best actors, gives an energetic, committed performance, the character never rises above a philandering boor.

Tom McCarthy’s “The Statement” is even more tiresome than Gilroy’s film. This numbing talkfest dramatizes a literal meeting that took place over three days in October 1980 at a Florida hotel. About 20 scientists and policymakers, appointed by the U.S. Congress, drafted a statement on carbon dioxide and climate change. The film offers some strong performances from John Turturro, Paul Rudd, and Paul Giamatti, but its drama is as boring as its premise sounds.

In my ranking of 2016 films, I put Ava DuVernay’s “13th” in the number one spot. This terrific documentary looked at the way the 13th Amendment, which abolished slavery, was misused to create a new form of slavery in the American prison system. The film earned and deserved widespread critical acclaim, but its sequel, “14th,” which premiered in the Closing Night slot at the NYFF, almost certainly won’t get the same general approbation. See Jourdain Searles’ review to find out why.

items.title: 'Our humble goal is to survive the AI revolution' says Epic Games CEO, as its Star Wars and Marvel crossover pivots to 'AI first' development
items.author: shaun.prescott@futurenet.com (Shaun Prescott)
items.summary: An unannounced Star Wars and Marvel shooter in the works at Epic Games has been delayed, and its creators instructed to take an "AI first" approach to
items.text:
An unannounced Star Wars and Marvel shooter in the works at Epic Games has been delayed, and its creators instructed to take an "AI first" approach to development. Staff were advised of the pivot last week, according to a Bloomberg report, with the project delayed indefinitely from its (unannounced) March 2027 release.

That "AI first" approach seems pretty comprehensive: the instructions per Bloomberg are to "implement an 'AI first' production model using tools such as Anthropic's Claude". Art will be "generated with full AI workflows", according to the same set of instructions.

Shortly after Bloomberg's report was published, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney took to X to share his own thoughts:

On AI use at Epic Games in general: "We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," he said. "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal."

On Epic 'not reading the room' when it comes to consumer attitudes towards generative AI: "Much of the room wants it to be 2016 again, but it's not. Our job, as the provider of tools and technology to much of the industry, is to design for the present that is and the future that will soon be. Personally I'm optimistic about it and see it as empowering for creators."

On whether Epic will "accelerate an IPO": "Our more modest aim is to survive the AI revolution, help other developers do the same, and come out on the other end making better code and content faster."

On potential improvements to development time offered by AI: "Right now it's highly variable, from 20% in some areas (like the most technical areas of UE [Unreal Engine] dev) to 5x for other areas (like web dev). By this time next year I expect very little will be less than 3x of January 2026 efficiency."

On AI's effects on game design in general: "The biggest change will be much faster time from having an idea to playtesting it. Let's be honest: a Marvel and Star Wars crossover shooter made by Epic Games, predominantly utilising generative AI and AI workflows, will be a pretty fascinating experiment to behold. People hated it when social media feeds stopped being feeds, so that, for example, weird videos about putting various objects through meat grinders are now mainstream. The transformation from "way to catch up with friends" into "ruinously addictive habit" wasn't appreciated, but it's the norm now anyway.

In other words, the tech industry knows that it doesn't matter whether you like it or not: you'll get what you're given.

Published Oct 14, 2026, 6:05 AM EDT

Thomas Butt is a senior writer. An avid film connoisseur, Thomas actively logs his film consumption on Letterboxd and vows to connect with many more cinephiles through the platform. He is immensely passionate about the work of Martin Scorsese, John Ford, and Albert Brooks. His work can be read on Collider and Taste of Cinema. He also writes for his own blog, The Empty Theater, on Substack. He is also a big fan of courtroom dramas and DVD commentary tracks. For Thomas, movie theaters are a second home. A native of Wakefield, MA, he is often found scrolling through the scheduled programming on Turner Classic Movies and making more room for his physical media collection. Thomas habitually increases his watchlist and jumps down a YouTube rabbit hole of archived interviews with directors and actors. He is inspired to write about film to uphold the medium's artistic value and to express his undying love for the art form. Thomas looks to cinema as an outlet to better understand the world, human emotions, and himself.

Just when we thought we were out, they pulled us back in. As the entire filmmaking industry shifts after the landmark merger between Paramount and Warner Bros., two of Hollywood's most iconic legacy studios, the trends that moviegoers embraced over the last year now face their greatest threat yet. 2025/2026 signaled a new era for the industry, headlined by two original movies, Sinners and Obsession, that became box office behemoths and cultural sensations. These films and other surprise hits, along with the disappointment of franchise films that were once considered financial guarantees, were supposed to be the catalysts for a new wave of movie-making that showed interest in fresh ideas, rather than sequels, IP, and old brands. But now, with the consolidation of studios and the subsequent increased influence of shareholders over studio output, the return of franchise omnipresence is a real threat to the industry's creative prosperity.

Skydance Owns a Vast Number of Brands and IP

Image via Warner Bros.

For decades, a corporate stranglehold has been growing on Hollywood, marked by the tech industry's foray into movie production and distribution. The Paramount-WB merger, now operating as Skydance, is the culmination of this unfortunate industry trend. Despite Skydance CEO David Ellison's claim that he is a "believer" in original storytelling, the company's upcoming movie lineup suggests that they are doubling down on safe, familiar franchises. Within no time, Deadline reported that the new mega studio had enlisted Stephen Spielberg and Michael Bay to revive the Transformers franchise.

The combined forces of Paramount and Warner Bros. result in a vast pool of IP ripe for further big-screen adaptations. Just to name a few, Skydance now has ownership of the aforementioned Transformers, DC Comics characters, Harry Potter, Star Trek, the Middle-earth saga, Barbie/Mattel, and many more. Each franchise has a new movie or series in the works, many of which were inherited from Warner Bros., such as The Batman: Part II, the Potter HBO series, and a rumored sequel to Greta Gerwig's 2023 mega blockbuster. It's hard to imagine that Paramount was pursuing a $110 billion acquisition of WB without wanting to capitalize on its lucrative properties, even if the company's newly developed indie/arthouse label, Clockwork, remains intact. Ellison and company have promised to give their major releases a proper theatrical release, but if the majority of their output is going to be franchise-oriented, then the business will be back to square one.

Serious question: have audiences just forgotten how to have fun at the movies?

Warner Bros.' final years as an autonomous studio will likely be remembered fondly by cinephiles — an era overseen by Michael De Luca and Pamela Abdy, who will not be part of Ellison's management team. At a time when the arts frequently capitulate to shareholders, De Luca and Abdy were among the last bastions of upholding creative freedom and backing auteur filmmakers in the major studio system. Under their leadership, Warner Bros. released a handful of original films that were both beloved and commercially successful, notably Sinners and Weapons, as well as the Best Picture-winning One Battle After Another. Of course, considering that they invested in polarizing movies with unconventional sensibilities, they also greenlit a fair share of noisy flops, including Mickey 17, The Bride!, and Digger, the latter of which released concurrently with the official approval of the merger.

A business merger of this magnitude doesn't go through to take financially reckless decisions, such as lending $100–200 million to Bong Joon-ho, Maggie Gyllenhaal, and Alejandro G. Iñárritu to make provocative black comedies with elaborate concepts and sets. And with all this IP under their belt, Skydance doesn't have to look too far to churn out a profit. While it appears that audiences will have to suffer from a continued onslaught of safe, predictable franchise entries and reboots, keep in mind that legacy brands and superheroes on their own no longer guarantee a blockbuster. Recent flops/financial disappointments like Supergirl, Scream 7, Masters of the Universe, and Star Wars: Mandalorian and Grogu suggest that audience tastes have moved on.

Box office numbers prove that most audiences want something familiar, but it has to present itself as fresh, as evidenced by the rise of new films with pre-established fanbases from other media like Minecraft and Backrooms. The media landscape is not too inspiring from afar, but if the market still dictates how decisions are made, then we can expect more breakthroughs like Sinners and Obsession.

items.title: 35 English Loanwords That Come From the Japanese Language
items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer
items.summary: While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly
items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Similarly, many aspects of Japanese entertainment tend to originate in Japan, and the English words borrowed from Japanese show that.

A lot of these loanwords are originally written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana. If you need to review hiragana and katakana, head to this article.

1. Karaoke (カラオケ)

Did you even know this was a Japanese word before Karaoke actually came into contact with Japan or the language? It has roots in the words: kara (空), meaning “empty,” and oke (オケ), meaning “orchestra.” So, together the word actually means orchestraAlso, have you seen anyone do karaoke like the Japanese?

2. Sudoku (すどく)

If you’ve played sudoku and understand it, more power to you. This game and its title originated in Japan in 1984 and have since become very popular worldwide. The su comes from suji or suu (数), meaning number, and the doku (独) means single. The overall aim of the game is to get numbers to appear once in squares in a grid. So literally, the numbers must remain single. Or suuji wa dokushin ni kagiru (数字は独身に限る), which was the original title of the game.

Europeans actually played a similar game in the 18th century. In the 1980s, a Japanese publisher distributed sudoku, which turned into a huge hit and has been popular ever since.

3. Pachinko　(パチンコ)

Hard to spend any time in Japan and not see a pachinko parlor. Pachinko is a kind of pinball game played in arcade games or, more commonly, gambling parlors. Japanese people like to make words that mimic or represent the sound you hear, like the bees buzzing or the snake hissing. The word pachinko is partly made up of a Japanese onomatopoeia. The first part, pachin, is from the sound that the metal pinball makes as it hits an obstacle. The ko is a diminutive suffix that means something like ‘little’.

4. Soy (sauce, beans)

Tofu and miso are obviously Japanese loanwords, but soy? Yes, apparently it comes from しょうゆ (shoyu), which is Japanese for soy sauce. The actual Japanese term for the bean is daizu. Edamame, which are green soybeans, is also commonly used in English.

5. Tamari (たまりしょうゆ)

This one is kind of hip these days. Many recipe bloggers suggest using tamari as a ‘healthy’ alternative to regular soy sauce. Tamari is richer, thicker, and less salty than regular soy sauce, but it is also made from fermented soybeans.

6. Shiitake, maitake, matsutake, and enoki mushrooms (椎茸、舞茸、松茸、えのき)

Did I miss any? Many Japanese mushroom names have been carried over and used as-is in English. The most popular of these might be shiitake, which is often pronounced without the second ‘i’, resulting in shitake.

7. Umami (旨味)

This Tiny Sardinian Village Might Be a New ‘Blue Zone’—and Could Hold the Secrets to Female Longevity

In Bolotana, a town on the Italian island with about 2,300 residents, women who reach the age of 70 are about three times as likely to live to 100 than women in the United States, according to a new study

Sarah Kuta
| Daily Correspondent

October 13, 2026 11:00 a.m.

A small village in the mountains of Sardinia may hold the secrets to female longevity.

In Bolotana, a town on the Italian island with about 2,300 residents, women who reach the age of 70 are about three times as likely to live to 100 than women in the United States, researchers report in a study published October 4 in the journal Frontiers in Aging.

The findings suggest Bolotana might be a previously unidentified “blue zone,” a place where people live exceptionally long lives. If confirmed, it would join destinations including another region of Sardinia; Okinawa, Japan; Ikaria, Greece; and Costa Rica’s Nicoya Peninsula as one of the world’s recognized longevity hotspots.

The study’s co-authors first learned of Bolotana because they heard about its abundance of centenarians, or people who live to be at least 100 years old.

Intrigued, the researchers decided to dig into the data. Using the town’s extensive historic records, which date back more than a century, they were able to independently verify the ages of Bolotana’s identified centenarians, living or dead. Of the 3,060 individuals born in Bolotana between 1900 and 1925, they confirmed that 38 lived to be at least 100.

Around the world, women tend to live longer than men. But the team’s analysis revealed that Bolotana’s female residents were exceptionally long-lived. In Bolotana, women who reach age 70 have a 13.83 percent chance of surviving to 100 years old, compared to just 4.92 percent for men. (That’s different from Sardinia’s original blue zone, which is known for male longevity.) For comparison, 70-year-old women across Italy have only a 3.5 percent chance of making it to 100, and in the U.S., that chance is 3.6 percent.

Once the women of Bolotana reach the age of 70, they have nearly 21 years of life remaining, based on the researchers’ estimates. The village appears to have one of the longest-lived female populations in the world, second only to Hong Kong.

The study doesn’t explain why Bolotana’s residents, particularly its women, lead such long lives—but the researchers have a few ideas. Community members eat little meat, and their largely plant-based diets consist primarily of foods they grow or make themselves, including wheat grown in their fields and cheese made from their sheep’s milk. They drink modest amounts of wine and consume a variety of olive oils.

Bolotana doesn’t have a gym, and its residents don’t exercise intentionally—but they do walk pretty much everywhere, including up and down the village’s steep, hilly streets. Additionally, Bolotana’s residents live in multi-generational households, and many men stay home and share in the household responsibilities.

Did you know? Long lives

In the United States, the life expectancy at birth is 81.4 years for women and 76.5 years for men.

Lead study author Giovanni Mario Pes, a longevity researcher at the University of Sassari in Italy, tells the Guardian’s Angela Giuffrida that Bolotana’s residents maintain “very intense and very real social relations” throughout their lives.

He pointed to Giovanna Marras, a 101-year-old woman who lives with her sister. “They live together, they cook together, they talk to each other easily,” Pes tells the Guardian. “There was absolutely no sign of cognitive decline.”

The team also suspects genetics might play a role, but they say they need to conduct more research to test that hypothesis.

However, they worry they will soon run out of time. If “cars, iPhones and American junk food” eventually reach the village, “you’ll see type 2 diabetes skyrocket, cardiovascular disease go up, dementia go up, many types of cancer go up, and the longevity phenomena will be gone,” study co-author Dan Buettner, a longevity researcher who founded the company Blue Zones and coined the term, tells National Geographic’s Jessica Roy. “I give it a generation. But … before that happens, we have a generation to bring our archaeological tools and uncover what they’ve been doing.”

Their research could have implications far beyond Bolotana, offering insights into the practices and values that might contribute to improving longevity across the globe.

“We now know something extraordinary is happening in Bolotana,” Buettner says in a statement. “The next step is to understand why and whether the lessons can help people elsewhere live longer, healthier lives.”

Some outside researchers have questioned the validity of the entire blue zones concept, pointing to unreliable birth records, potential age misreporting, methodological shortcomings and the team’s commercial interests.

However, Pes says the new research provides strong evidence that Bolotana’s residents have lived to unusually advanced ages.

“It is not just the level of longevity in Bolotana that is remarkable, but the degree to which it can be reconstructed from independent historical sources,” he says in the statement. “When civil records, parish archives and family lineages all converge on the same individuals across more than a century, it allows us to rigorously test longevity patterns in a way that is rarely possible in demography.”

items.title: The Underground Art of Traditional Japanese Tattooing
items.author: Wakaba Oto
items.summary: There are many ways to look at a dragon. In The Japanese Tattoo, a new photobook by writer and photographer Manami Okazaki, one can begin with the obvious
items.text:
There are many ways to look at a dragon. In The Japanese Tattoo, a new photobook by writer and photographer Manami Okazaki, one can begin with the obvious pleasures: the curve of its body across a man’s back, the dense black of sumi ink sunk deep into skin, the waves and clouds that carry it from shoulder to thigh. Across 240 pages, Okazaki documents wabori — the Japanese tradition of large-scale, often full-body tattooing — in sumptuous detail.

There is another way of looking, though: outward. Beyond the dragon is the body that carries it; beyond the body, the horishi — the tattoo master — who made it; behind his hands, generations of others. Okazaki’s photographs keep widening the frame, from finished bodysuits to the people and places around them, while archival photographs and woodblock prints reach backward into the working-class culture of Edo-period Tokyo.

That wider world is what has occupied Okazaki for nearly two decades. She has been documenting Japanese tattoo culture since 2007, returning to many of the same masters as they have aged, retired and, in some cases, died. Her new book is both a record of their work and an attempt to place it back inside the culture that produced it.

Horishi / Tattoo Artist Horikazu. Photograph by Cory Lum

A First Encounter With Japanese Tattoos

Okazaki’s own introduction to that world came almost by accident. Raised in Australia but accustomed to spending summers in Japan, she was 18 and fresh out of high school when she found a book on traditional tattooing and decided she wanted one herself. Knowing little about its customs, she committed what, in retrospect, she realizes was a faux pas: She cold-called one of the country’s most renowned horishi.

“I was completely clueless and knew nothing. You don’t just call someone like that out of the blue,” she says now.

He was booked for months; she had 10 days before her flight to Thailand. Something about the absurdity of the request amused him enough that he agreed to tattoo her at 2 a.m. He still remembers her, she says, largely because of how ridiculous the whole thing was.

What she recalls most clearly from that first encounter, though, is not the tattoo itself. “It wasn’t just the fact of getting tattooed,” she says. “It was my first encounter with a Japanese artisan.”

Photograph by Cory Lum

The Low City: Tattooing in Edo

“A tattoo isn’t just the thing you put on your body,” Okazaki says. “Even the process of going to the horishi, then going to the sento afterwards, then getting tattooed specifically for matsuri — it’s all part of the lifestyle of downtown. It’s all integrated. It’s a culture and a context.”

In The Japanese Tattoo, Okazaki reconstructs the social history behind the images, tracing wabori to the commoner culture of Edo and particularly shitamachi, the historically working-class “low city” of merchants, artisans and laborers in what is now eastern Tokyo. Her book makes the case that wabori was never simply a visual style, nor did it carry a single fixed meaning. It took its significance from the lives of the people who wore it: their work, their allegiances, their ideas about status, beauty, danger and death. To understand the tattoo, in other words, requires looking beyond its imagery to the social conditions that made that imagery meaningful.

Edo’s firefighters offer one example. Fire was an ordinary terror in a city built largely of wood, and commoner brigades fought it by climbing onto roofs and tearing down buildings before the flames could spread. Rival brigades competed for prestige, and firefighters became working-class celebrities known as much for their bravado as their tattoos, worn as a sign of both masculinity and trade. Dragons, creatures associated with water and thought to bring rain, were an especially fitting motif for men who routinely entered the flames.

Protective imagery remains common among people in dangerous trades. One veteran horishi interviewed by Okazaki recalls tattooing firefighters, carpenters and construction workers. Men who work at dangerous heights, he tells her, sometimes choose a hawk after seeing co-workers fall to their deaths; the hope is that, should they fall themselves, they will fly.

Photograph by Cory Lum

Notes From Underground: Tattoos and the Yakuza

The yakuza made something different of wabori. Tattoos could mark initiation, intimidate and confer status. Even individual motifs carried particular meanings: Koi, meaning carp, is a near-homophone for the Japanese command “come whenever” — read among yakuza as a vow to be ready to die at any moment, the same readiness expected of the men who wear it.

In The Japanese Tattoo, the horishi Horitoku, who spent decades tattooing yakuza clients in Tokyo, tells Okazaki that bosses would send younger members to him by introduction. Each would announce his group affiliation and rank when he arrived. A good tattoo mattered inside prison, too, he says: With every inmate dressed alike, wabori became one of the few ways to distinguish oneself, and exceptional work could earn even a low-ranking gangster the respect of his superiors.

By the 1970s, yakuza patronage was substantial enough that some horishi spent weeks traveling Japan to tattoo entire groups, with the organizations covering their expenses. Horiyoshi III, the influential Yokohama master, estimates that gangsters once made up around 60% of his clients. Today, he puts the figure at almost zero. Anti-organized crime laws, changing attitudes and the tattoo boom of the late 1990s and 2000s transformed that relationship. Some prominent horishi now refuse gang-affiliated clients altogether.

As the link between wabori and organized crime has started to fray, tattoos are slowly — very slowly — gaining acceptance in Japanese society. Part of that shifting stigma, Okazaki says, is related to the rise of tattooing as fashion. “Once something becomes pure fashion, it loses some of the subversive, underground appeal that attracted people to it in the first place,” she says.

Photograph by Cory Lum

The Last of Their Kind

Nearly two decades into documenting Japanese tattoo culture, Okazaki finds herself working with a much smaller circle of traditional masters. The Japanese Tattoo consequently turns its attention to a handful of them in unusual depth. “The people I focused on felt like the last of their kind,” she says.

What may disappear with them is more than a mere technique. It is a set of values that Okazaki traces to iki, an Edo ideal of urban sophistication that prized restraint. The idea arose partly out of necessity: Sumptuary laws barred commoners from conspicuous displays of luxury, so extravagance retreated to wherever inspectors weren’t looking, most famously into kimono linings, where a sober exterior might conceal silk dense with color and pattern. Over time, discretion itself became an expression of taste.

Traditional wabori reflects the same values. A full bodysuit can demand years of work and extraordinary commitment, only to disappear completely beneath ordinary clothes. Horicho II, a veteran tattooist, makes the comparison explicit: Wabori, he says, is like the pattern hidden inside a kimono. “It is beautiful because you only get a glimpse of it.”

The analogy extends to the people who make the tattoos. While tattooists elsewhere, and increasingly in the internet age, may cultivate the persona of artist or celebrity, the masters Okazaki documents tend to describe themselves as craftsmen. Their expertise extends beyond the mechanics of tattooing to the cultural knowledge behind the images themselves. Horitoku explains that reproducing a figure from an Edo-period print requires knowing how its obi is tied, why its sleeves fall as they do and what kind of wig he wears. The Tokyo-based master encourages younger tattooists to attend kabuki and sumo and study these details for themselves.

This is why Okazaki is wary of treating preservation as simply keeping an old visual style alive. Wabori has never been static: Her first tattoo book, published in 2008, featured traditional masters alongside artists incorporating influences from elsewhere. The question is whether the knowledge behind the images proves as durable as the images themselves.

“The beauty of Japanese tattooing comes from the way people live,” she says. “I hope wabori remains a real craft, not just a style. It doesn’t have to stay stuck in the Edo period, but the culture behind it matters.”

items.text:
On a sun-drenched summer afternoon, I accompany Ema Gaspar to one of her go-to studios: Kiyosumi Park. It’s an unassuming local green space, one that most people would walk right past, but in her eyes, it’s an enchanted forest teeming with characters waiting to be brought to life. Sitting on a wooden bench, she pulls out a sketchbook and a couple of colored pencils from a tote bag and begins sketching without much ceremony — faint, downy patches of purple and green that slowly form a wide-eyed creature with a butterfly’s coiling mouth and leaves for ears.

“I like to understand the personality of plants and flowers, and then create their own fashion sense,” the illustrator explains. “I think to myself, ‘What kind of clothes would this flower like? What kind of brand would this flower like?’” Her plant spirits are often clad in girly-grunge silhouettes and groovy patterns, captured with a combination of childlike whimsy and sleek hyperpop maximalism. Gaspar’s style calls to mind a range of influences — 60s psychedelia, the anime series Digimon, Y2K Harajuku fashion as chronicled in the pages of Fruits magazine — which explains its strong resonance with Zillennials rediscovering their analog childhoods.

The distinct charm of her illustrated world has reached an impressive roster of clients and fans over the years. In addition to creating cover art and visuals for musicians — Gracie Abrams, Mura Masa and Mei Semones, to name a few — she’s done high-profile collaborations with brands like Hysteric Glamour, Coyseio and Heaven by Marc Jacobs, designing merchandise worn by the likes of Bella Hadid, Blackpink’s Jennie and members of NewJeans. Recently, Gaspar took one of the most reproduced symbols of all time — the Nike swoosh — and revamped it with her signature swirling florals for a kidswear line.

Her rise also coincides with something bigger. More and more luxury brands — Hermès, Loewe, Dior Beauty — have been courting independent illustrators and animators for campaigns that might have gone to, say, a photographer or a design studio a few years back. Why? Because, against a never-ending current of AI slop, connotations of originality, effort and slowness have become increasingly scarce (and therefore lucrative). Gaspar isn’t naive to the reasons behind this new demand for handmade art, but is disinclined to overthink it; she’s mostly just amazed and grateful to have achieved her dream job.

Conversations With Plants

Gaspar is Portuguese and did all her schooling in Lisbon, studying painting at university. One of her earliest memories, she says, is sitting in her grandparents’ garden with a pen and paper. “I used to go there and talk with plants,” she recalls. “My childhood wasn’t that easy, so drawing helped me a lot through stuff.”

She did “a lot of random jobs” before her work took off around 2020, during the pandemic, which gave her the time to really focus on her illustrations. Moving to Tokyo in 2023 was partially career-motivated: She had done an artist residency at Studio Kura in Itoshima a few years back and built relationships in Tokyo, even holding a brief solo exhibition. It was also a childhood dream, based on her love of Japanese pop culture and her grandfather’s stories of travel.

“It was a big change because Lisbon, and Portugal in general, are very chill places — which is good for me,” Gaspar notes. “It took a little bit of time to like being in a city where everything is so quick.”

To maintain her peace, she goes to parks around her home every day, listens to ambient music, cooks regularly and tries to have dinners with friends as often as possible. Gaspar’s most recent solo exhibition, titled “Paku Paku” (a Japanese onomatopoeia for gobbling up food), reflects the inspiration she derives from these dinners. “When we’re eating and talking about our life problems, I feel healed from within,” she explains.

As an illustrator, Gaspar aims to create this “safe space of inspiration” for others. It’s why she launched Plant Drawing Club, a free workshop in which she draws and colors with friends and fans. “It’s a bit therapeutic — people have even cried during the workshops! But in a good way,” she says. “We get so focused on our routines and working that we forget about how we feel, what we like, connecting with ourselves and others. It’s very important nowadays to do that.”

The Human Touch

Gaspar’s earnest dedication to vulnerability and connection is at the core of her ethos; these values are particularly important to her as an artist in an increasingly AI-driven world. “When you see artwork made by an illustrator, you can see the whole process when they show the final piece,” she suggests. “It’s very fragile — that fragility is what makes us human.”

She also understands that this elusive “human” quality is what makes illustrators so attractive to brands and consumers right now. “Art is always connected with society itself and society’s needs,” she says. “Brands want the client to feel connected on a personal level, and independent illustrators can bring that — a sense of personality, a sense of human touch.”

Luckily, the eternal artist’s dilemma — how much of your style to water down for a client — is rarely an issue for Gaspar. “Usually, when brands reach out to me, they already know my style and are prepared for [the final product] to be a bit crazy,” she explains, laughing. Transporting her characters into a client’s vision is usually a fun challenge: discovering new ways to cast her whimsical, pastel-toned lens on the emotions of a song, the mood of a runway collection, a brand’s aesthetic codes.

“Every job I have with brands feels like a gift to me,” Gaspar says. “I always wanted illustration to be my job, but coming from Portugal, it’s hard for that to happen. It wasn’t something that I believed 100%; it was just a hope.”

It’s possible that corporations are commissioning illustrators like Gaspar for optics; the sudden demand for a decidedly human touch may not necessarily coincide with a genuine desire to prioritize substance over efficiency. (The same Nike that commissioned Gaspar, for example, recently caught flak for recruiting a “generative AI lead designer” for its footwear.) Still, the phenomenon feels like a net positive. Artists are getting paid, and audiences are encountering talent they might not have found on their own. Like so many things that felt obsolete a decade ago — print magazines, dinner parties, wired headphones shared with a friend — illustration is having a renaissance that suggests that physical presence is more precious than ever amid an endless quest for convenience and optimization.

As we part ways at the park, Gaspar hands me her completed drawing of the plant creature, tearing out the sketchbook page while apologizing profusely for not offering something to put it in. Grainy, softly gradient and carefree in the way only colored pencil drawings can be, its self-contained joy reminds me of my own childhood doodles. I roll up the paper and hold it in my hand the whole train ride home like a baby bird, careful not to dent its delicate frame.

items.title: Why Japan’s Traditional Wagashi Shops Are Going Bankrupt at a Record Pace
items.author: Eugenie Shin
items.summary: For centuries, Japan’s wagashi — traditional sweets most often made of azuki red bean paste, rice flour and sugar — have been deeply embedded in Japanese
items.text:
For centuries, Japan’s wagashi — traditional sweets most often made of azuki red bean paste, rice flour and sugar — have been deeply embedded in Japanese culture. Artfully crafted to reflect the subtle changing of the seasons, the delicate treats are central to gift-giving and often accompany traditional tea ceremonies.

Yet today, the historic shops that specialize in wagashi are closing at a record pace. According to new data from Teikoku Databank, 22 wagashi makers filed for bankruptcy between January and September 2026. This puts the year on pace to beat 2025’s record, the highest since Teikoku Databank’s records begin in 2000.

Notably, these closures are disproportionately affecting long-established businesses. Over half of the shops that have gone bankrupt since 2020 were operating for more than 50 years, and nearly 18% were over a century old. Well-known regional brands, such as Ishikawa Prefecture’s Takasagoya and Kanagawa’s Izumiya, have already went bankrupt.

Rising Costs and Shifting Consumer Habits

At the heart of the crisis is the financial strain caused by increasing production costs and an inability to raise prices accordingly. The costs of essential ingredients — specifically azuki beans, sugar and glutinous rice — have risen steadily, alongside higher costs for packaging, utilities and staff wages.

However, wagashi shop owners face strong consumer resistance to price hikes. Unlike Western pastries, which Japanese shoppers tend to view as luxury indulgences, wagashi are seen as affordable everyday items or modest gifts. As a result, shops that raised prices suffered a drop in sales, while those that kept prices unchanged despite rising costs were forced to absorb severe losses.

Shifting consumer habits are also to blame. Traditional formal gift-giving customs are becoming less common, and young people are buying fewer wagashi than older generations.

At the same time, master wagashi artisans — shokunin — are retiring without successors, leaving heritage houses with no one trained to carry on the craft. Alongside these hurdles, many owners are also struggling under heavy debt, both from pandemic-era relief loans and recent investments in new store and factory facilities.

Preserving the Craft and Embracing the New

Despite these challenges, some wagashi makers are finding ways to adapt. Teikoku Databank points to several strategies that are working.

The most visible is product development aimed at younger customers. A growing number of shops are making “neo-wagashi,” sweets that pair traditional ingredients with modern flavors, photogenic designs and new textures, such as red bean paste combined with chocolate. Others are using trending items like fruit-filled daifuku and warabimochi to bring in customers who might never have bought a traditional box of sweets.

Some shops have moved into tourist areas to draw international visitors, and others now make sweets under contract for convenience stores and supermarkets. The tradeoff is that the shop’s name usually doesn’t appear on the package, so the work brings in revenue but does little for the brand.

Some are going online, both through their own shops and through furusato nozei, Japan’s hometown tax donation program. Under the system, taxpayers can donate to a municipality of their choice, deduct most of the donation from their income and residence taxes and receive a thank-you gift from that municipality, often a local food specialty. For a regional wagashi maker, being chosen as one of those gifts means its sweets go to donors across the country, many of whom would never have walked past the shop.

These trends suggest that relying on historical reputation alone may no longer be enough in an evolving market. As customer habits and costs shift, the future for wagashi makers appears increasingly tied to how well they can preserve their core craftsmanship while finding new ways to connect with modern buyers.

items.title: How Long Does It Take to Learn Japanese? (Honest Answer)
items.author: Coto Academy Teachers
items.summary: If you have started learning Japanese or thinking about doing it soon, you might ask yourself: How long does it take to learn Japanese? It’s an honest
items.text:
If you have started learning Japanese or thinking about doing it soon, you might ask yourself: How long does it take to learn Japanese? It’s an honest question, and probably the most important. Between people’s fascination with Japanese culture and the desire to live in Japan, Japanese has become one of the most popular languages to learn – but also the hardest, too.

The answer to this question is, “it depends”. Understandably, no one likes to hear that — but it’s an honest answer because there’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to how long it takes to learn Japanese. On a complete beginner-to-advanced scale, it takes around 180 to 1,2000 hours to learn Japanese. In reality, people with no prior kanji knowledge often take more time to learn Japanese thanthose who have.

In this response, we’ll explore the factors that can affect how long it takes to learn Japanese and provide estimates of how long it may take a beginner to become proficient.

Defining Fluency in Japanese Language Learning

To the majority, language fluency is a spectrum. You can talk to your Japanese friends in casual Japanese and call it fluent. You might think that to be one means being able to lead a meeting with your coworkers in full keigo.

A good rule of thumb is if you find yourself constantly translating between Japanese and your own native language and forming sentences quickly, you’d be hard-pressed to describe yourself as fluent. In its academic definition, made by Dr. Paul Nation and Asuza Yamamoto, fluency is ‘being able to receive and produce language at a reasonable rate’. You should ask yourself, “Am I at ease when I speak Japanese? Do I get constantly worried about the next question from my partner?”

On the other hand, this number begs the question: Can I call myself fluent if I can watch anime without subtitles? Can I talk to my Japanese friends without fillers like eto or ano? Or write a foolproof business email to your Japanese boss?

Remember that there’s more to communication than speaking and listening! Japanese language fluency also includes four aspects: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. You may be excellent at conversing in Japanese, but barely able to write a single kanji.

So depending on how you define fluency, you might get to that point faster or slower! And don’t worry: we’ve broken down the study hours based on your goal and the desired level below.

How Long Does it Take to Learn Japanese Based on Your Goal?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. This is probably a fairer assessment than saying it takes 2 years to speak Japanese. The more hours you put into practicing Japanese in a day or stay consistent throughout the week, the faster you’ll learn.

Ultimately, achieving a high level in Japanese takes time, as with other languages. A lot of people who live in Japan and studied the language for years might still say they have a long way to go, so you can’t expect instant results in a matter of weeks.

As a reference, we’ve broken down how long it takes to learn Japanese based on what you’re using the language for. Depending on your goal, you might want to focus on one language aspect (like speaking) more than the other.

GoalHow you’ll use JapaneseStudy Hours

TravelAsk for directions, order food, and make basic greetings.7 – 30 days

Make friendsDaily conversations, expressing thoughts and opinions, holding natural conversations in a wider range of circumstances.900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

Work part-time job in JapanSpeak basic keigo to customers, interact with Japanese coworkers900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)

Get a job in JapanTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination) and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, and make a presentation2,000 – 4,000 study hours (2 years)

Go to universityTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination, and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, make a presentationUse keigo (Japanese honorifics), business Japanese, manners, and cultural awareness, JLPT (N2 or N1)

How Many Hours a Day Should You Study Japanese

You might notice we’ve been using “study hours” instead of exact days or months, which can be frustrating if you want a straightforward answer on how long it takes to learn Japanese.

Days and months can vary in length and can be influenced by external factors, such as holidays or personal schedules, making it difficult to accurately track progress. There are people who might study 30 minutes a day. Some dedicate 3 hours a day, while a few people spend 6-7 hours studying full-time. This isn’t the best standardized unit of time.

If you are learning as a hobby, dedicating 15 to 30 minutes a day to studying is fine. In 6 months, you’ll be able to read basic texts and hold limited conversations.

Most people recommend studying for 3 to 4 hours every day on a set schedule, which allows your brain to work at its full capacity and avoid burnout. Even intensive courses at Coto Academy and Japanese language classes at other Japanese language schools only have 3-hour classes on weekdays.

So if you think studying 9 hours a day to achieve the “study hour goal” is a good idea, think again! You’ll most likely experience burnout and have trouble holding onto the information that you have learned.

Head here full our guide on how long it takes to study for each JLPT level!

How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Beginner

When we think of Japanese levels, we tend to associate it with JLPT, or the Japanese Language Proficiency Test, as the ultimate benchmark for how much Japanese you know. Beginner-level Japanese ranges from JLPT N5 (beginner) to N4 (upper beginner).

According to the official JLPT administrator, JLPT N5 and N4 “prove your ability to understand some basic Japanese.” You should be able to listen and comprehend conversations about daily life and classroom situations — provided that they are spoken slowly.

Reading-wise, this means you’re already familiar with daily topics written in basic vocabulary and kanji.

For students with kanji knowledge, it takes 350 study hours to pass JLPT N5, and 462 hours if you have no prior kanji knowledge. For JLPT N4, it will take 550 hours and 787 hours under the same conditions.

Keep in mind that the JLPT does not test your conversational skills, so while your written Japanese skills are good, this doesn’t necessarily reflect your practical fluency during day-to-day conversations.

If you want to learn the most basic kanji and have no prior experience with Japanese, it should take you around a month. This is if you learn 10 kanji a day every day.

How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Intermediate

Japanese intermediate level is around JLPT N3, which can take 900 – 1,500 study hours to get to. Many Japanese learners are at this level, and you should be able to get a part-time job at this point. You are able to get around Japan with ease, and while you may still encounter difficulties in understanding and expressing certain ideas, you should be able to engage in conversations on a wide range of topics with a degree of fluency and accuracy.

Typically, studying for JLPT N3 takes about 6 months to one year, depending on how many hours you dedicate each day and how hard you commit to your study plan.

Around N3, you should already know around 650 kanji, which can take anywhere from 2 months to four months if you learn 5-10 kanji each day.

How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Advanced

In order to get a high level of Japanese proficiency for work, you’ll want to achieve JLPT N1 and have sufficient written and spoken ability to effectively communicate in various settings, such as in-person interactions, emails, presentations, and meetings, with a mastery of the formal Japanese register (keigo). Acquiring the JLPT N2 or N1 certification can take anywhere from 2,200 hours to 3,900 hours of study, which would require at least 2 years of full-time study. Even after obtaining an N1 certification, many learners continue to study more kanji and vocabulary to further improve their proficiency.

You can achieve the same advanced level in 3-5 years of learning Japanese part-time. This is when you can get jobs that require native-level Japanese skills, like interpreters, translators, customer service, and Japanese teachers.

In most cases, the amount of exposure to the Japanese language and culture plays a big part in truly reaching an advanced level. At this point, it’s not just about knowing a lot of grammar points, vocabulary, or kanji; it’s also about understanding the culture and context in which the language is used.

Ways to Speed up Japanese Learning

Most of us have different learning preferences, like taking notes, using visuals or graphics, or speaking words out loud. There are numerous ways to acquire proficiency in Japanese, but selecting the most effective method for yourself will enable you to enhance your learning speed and quality. Here are a few tips we always recommend to those who are starting to learn Japanese.

1. Find a language partner

Studying alone can be boring unless you’re an introvert. Not only does it provide an opportunity to practice speaking and listening in a natural setting, but it also offers insight into Japanese culture, values, and customs. Interacting with native speakers can expose you to a variety of regional dialects, idiomatic expressions, and slang that are not commonly found in textbooks or language courses. Moreover, it allows you to receive immediate feedback on your language usage, pronunciation, and grammar, which is invaluable in accelerating your language acquisition.

Engaging in conversations with Japanese friends or exchange partners can also make language learning more enjoyable, provide new social connections, and lead to a deeper understanding and appreciation of Japanese culture. We recommend checking out our curated list of Japanese language exchange apps and where to find language exchange events.

2. Study Japanese in Japan for Total Immersion

This one is probably obvious, but hear us out: you learn Japanese most effectively when you’re studying the language in Japan — or at least when you are constantly exposed to Japanese culture. Besides, what better way to reward yourself for your hard work than to visit a country we all love?

Immersing yourself in Japanese culture and making friends with native speakers can be almost impossible outside Japan. Being in Japan will boost your progress considerably. You’re conditioned to always use Japanese, and you’ll inevitably hear Japanese words and phrases every day.

3. Define your motivation and goal

Want to learn Japanese as a hobby? Find new job opportunities in Japan from overseas? Watch your favorite anime. It’s good to define your goal in learning Japanese for a couple of reasons; the first being that these goals are your motivators. A lot of people lose interest in learning Japanese because it gets too hard or boring. Knowing why you want to study in the first place helps you to keep the traction going.

Second, and probably more importantly, it helps you identify which language element you need to focus on. Learning Japanese to take the JLPT for university entrance? You should do a well-balanced study plan covering listening, speaking, reading, and vocabulary. Want to be able to make small talk? Try to do more conversation practice instead.

4. Use a mix of Japanese study materials

Perhaps you’re an auditory learner. Or maybe you notice you hate using textbooks. No matter what kind of Japanese learner you are, studying Japanese can be more effective when you’re genuinely enjoying it — or even making it fun!

And the good news is, you can learn from things you already enjoy in Japanese. For example, if you like playing video games, you can switch the language to Japanese, especially with games like Pokémon, where the language is simple and easy to change when starting a new game.

Enjoy reading manga? Challenge yourself to read a bit each day in Japanese, and as you progress, it will become easier. Additionally, watching your favorite shows in Japanese, like anime series or Terrace House on Netflix, is a fun way to pick up new vocabulary and slang. Initially, try watching without subtitles and actively listening, taking notes, and then watching again with subtitles on to see what you understood and learned.

We have a huge list of articles dedicated to different learning resources: Anki, podcasts, YouTube, TikToks and TV shows, so check them out on our blog!

5. Join a Japanese course

It’s important not to overlook the significance of getting the right professional support and establishing a study routine. This is where taking a Japanese course comes in.

One of the main benefits of taking a Japanese class is having access to a qualified instructor who can answer questions, provide feedback, and offer guidance tailored to your individual needs. Additionally, studying with a group of peers can create a sense of accountability and motivation, as well as the opportunity to practice speaking and listening skills with others.

If you’re considering taking a Japanese class, we recommend checking out Coto Academy. They offer a wide range of courses, from beginner to advanced levels, taught by experienced and knowledgeable instructors. Their curriculum is designed to be engaging and interactive, and they use a variety of teaching methods to cater to different learning styles. Additionally, their flexible scheduling options and online classes make it easy to fit language learning into your busy schedule.


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


Conclusion

Learning to speak Japanese involves many factors, but by developing good study habits, managing your time effectively, and staying committed, you can become conversational in a few months. This may come as a surprise, as you may have had different expectations about the process of learning Japanese.

It’s important to find joy and a sense of satisfaction throughout your journey, not just at the end goal. Celebrate each small accomplishment along the way and try not to focus too much on how far you still have to go. One day, you’ll be glad that you persevered and didn’t give up!

How long does it take to learn Japanese for beginners?


The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. However, the amount of time it takes to learn Japanese for beginners depends on various factors, such as how often and how long you study, the quality of your study materials, your motivation, and your natural ability to learn languages.

How many hours a day should I study Japanese to become fluent?

The number of hours a day you need to study Japanese to become fluent depends on your personal goals, your current level of proficiency, and your preferred learning style. Generally, it’s recommended to study at least 1-2 hours a day, every day, to make steady progress. As a reference, intensive Japanese courses typically 3 hours a day. Studying 6 hours or more in a day may lead to burnout.

Can I become fluent in Japanese in six months?


While it’s possible to make significant progress in six months of intensive study, becoming fully fluent in Japanese within such a short period is unlikely. Achieving fluency in Japanese requires a deep understanding of the language, which takes time to develop. You can achieve conversational fluency in six months.

How long does it take to pass the JLPT N5, N4, N3, N2 or N1 level?


On average, it takes 6 months to 1 year of dedicated study to pass each level of the JLPT. However, some people may take longer or shorter depending on their individual circumstances.

Can I learn Japanese faster with a tutor or language exchange partner?


Working with a tutor or language exchange partner can help you learn Japanese faster and more effectively. A tutor can provide personalized instruction and feedback, while a language exchange partner can offer opportunities to practice speaking and listening skills with a native speaker.

How long does it take to learn Japanese kanji?


On average, it takes about 2-3 years of consistent study to master the basic set of 2,136 Joyo kanji (commonly used characters in Japan).

Can I learn Japanese on my own without a teacher?


Yes, it’s possible to learn Japanese on your own without a teacher. However, self-study requires a lot of discipline, motivation, and the right resources. You’ll need to find quality textbooks, online resources, and study materials, and you’ll need to develop a consistent study routine to make progress.

Is it difficult to learn Japanese compared to other languages?


Japanese is considered to be a logical and consistent language with a relatively simple sound system, but it’s considered one of the hardest languages to learn for English speakers. FSI considered Japanese a “super-hard language”, categorizing it in the same group as Arabic, Korean, Mandarin, and Cantonese.

blocks.x: If you have started learning Japanese or thinking about doing it soon, you might ask yourself: How long does it take to learn Japanese? It’s an honest question, and probably the most important. Between people’s fascination with Japanese culture and the desire to live in Japan, Japanese has become one of the most popular languages to learn – but also the hardest, too.

The answer to this question is, “it depends”. Understandably, no one likes to hear that — but it’s an honest answer because there’s no one-size-fits-all when it comes to how long it takes to learn Japanese. On a complete beginner-to-advanced scale, it takes around 180 to 1,2000 hours to learn Japanese. In reality, people with no prior kanji knowledge often take more time to learn Japanese thanthose who have.
In this response, we’ll explore the factors that can affect how long it takes to learn Japanese and provide estimates of how long it may take a beginner to become proficient.
Defining Fluency in Japanese Language Learning

To the majority, language fluency is a spectrum. You can talk to your Japanese friends in casual Japanese and call it fluent. You might think that to be one means being able to lead a meeting with your coworkers in full keigo.

A good rule of thumb is if you find yourself constantly translating between Japanese and your own native language and forming sentences quickly, you’d be hard-pressed to describe yourself as fluent. In its academic definition, made by Dr. Paul Nation and Asuza Yamamoto, fluency is ‘being able to receive and produce language at a reasonable rate’. You should ask yourself, “Am I at ease when I speak Japanese? Do I get constantly worried about the next question from my partner?”

On the other hand, this number begs the question: Can I call myself fluent if I can watch anime without subtitles? Can I talk to my Japanese friends without fillers like eto or ano? Or write a foolproof business email to your Japanese boss?

Remember that there’s more to communication than speaking and listening! Japanese language fluency also includes four aspects: speaking, listening, reading, and writing. You may be excellent at conversing in Japanese, but barely able to write a single kanji.
So depending on how you define fluency, you might get to that point faster or slower! And don’t worry: we’ve broken down the study hours based on your goal and the desired level below.
How Long Does it Take to Learn Japanese Based on Your Goal?

The FSI of the US State Department estimates that it takes 88 weeks, or 2,200 study hours, to reach what most people define as Japanese fluency. This is probably a fairer assessment than saying it takes 2 years to speak Japanese. The more hours you put into practicing Japanese in a day or stay consistent throughout the week, the faster you’ll learn.

Ultimately, achieving a high level in Japanese takes time, as with other languages. A lot of people who live in Japan and studied the language for years might still say they have a long way to go, so you can’t expect instant results in a matter of weeks.

As a reference, we’ve broken down how long it takes to learn Japanese based on what you’re using the language for. Depending on your goal, you might want to focus on one language aspect (like speaking) more than the other.
GoalHow you’ll use JapaneseStudy Hours
TravelAsk for directions, order food, and make basic greetings.7 – 30 days
Make friendsDaily conversations, expressing thoughts and opinions, holding natural conversations in a wider range of circumstances.900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)
Work part-time job in JapanSpeak basic keigo to customers, interact with Japanese coworkers900-1,300 study hours (6 months – 1 year)
Get a job in JapanTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination) and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, and make a presentation2,000 – 4,000 study hours (2 years)

Go to universityTake the EJU (Japanese entrance examination, and JLPT (N2 or N1), take Japanese tests, make a presentationUse keigo (Japanese honorifics), business Japanese, manners, and cultural awareness, JLPT (N2 or N1)
How Many Hours a Day Should You Study Japanese
You might notice we’ve been using “study hours” instead of exact days or months, which can be frustrating if you want a straightforward answer on how long it takes to learn Japanese.

Days and months can vary in length and can be influenced by external factors, such as holidays or personal schedules, making it difficult to accurately track progress. There are people who might study 30 minutes a day. Some dedicate 3 hours a day, while a few people spend 6-7 hours studying full-time. This isn’t the best standardized unit of time.
If you are learning as a hobby, dedicating 15 to 30 minutes a day to studying is fine. In 6 months, you’ll be able to read basic texts and hold limited conversations.

Most people recommend studying for 3 to 4 hours every day on a set schedule, which allows your brain to work at its full capacity and avoid burnout. Even intensive courses at Coto Academy and Japanese language classes at other Japanese language schools only have 3-hour classes on weekdays.

So if you think studying 9 hours a day to achieve the “study hour goal” is a good idea, think again! You’ll most likely experience burnout and have trouble holding onto the information that you have learned.
Head here full our guide on how long it takes to study for each JLPT level!
How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Beginner

When we think of Japanese levels, we tend to associate it with JLPT, or the Japanese Language Proficiency Test, as the ultimate benchmark for how much Japanese you know. Beginner-level Japanese ranges from JLPT N5 (beginner) to N4 (upper beginner).

According to the official JLPT administrator, JLPT N5 and N4 “prove your ability to understand some basic Japanese.” You should be able to listen and comprehend conversations about daily life and classroom situations — provided that they are spoken slowly.
Reading-wise, this means you’re already familiar with daily topics written in basic vocabulary and kanji.

For students with kanji knowledge, it takes 350 study hours to pass JLPT N5, and 462 hours if you have no prior kanji knowledge. For JLPT N4, it will take 550 hours and 787 hours under the same conditions.

Keep in mind that the JLPT does not test your conversational skills, so while your written Japanese skills are good, this doesn’t necessarily reflect your practical fluency during day-to-day conversations.
If you want to learn the most basic kanji and have no prior experience with Japanese, it should take you around a month. This is if you learn 10 kanji a day every day.
How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Intermediate

Japanese intermediate level is around JLPT N3, which can take 900 – 1,500 study hours to get to. Many Japanese learners are at this level, and you should be able to get a part-time job at this point. You are able to get around Japan with ease, and while you may still encounter difficulties in understanding and expressing certain ideas, you should be able to engage in conversations on a wide range of topics with a degree of fluency and accuracy.
Typically, studying for JLPT N3 takes about 6 months to one year, depending on how many hours you dedicate each day and how hard you commit to your study plan.
Around N3, you should already know around 650 kanji, which can take anywhere from 2 months to four months if you learn 5-10 kanji each day.
How Long it Takes to Learn Japanese: Advanced

In order to get a high level of Japanese proficiency for work, you’ll want to achieve JLPT N1 and have sufficient written and spoken ability to effectively communicate in various settings, such as in-person interactions, emails, presentations, and meetings, with a mastery of the formal Japanese register (keigo). Acquiring the JLPT N2 or N1 certification can take anywhere from 2,200 hours to 3,900 hours of study, which would require at least 2 years of full-time study. Even after obtaining an N1 certification, many learners continue to study more kanji and vocabulary to further improve their proficiency.

You can achieve the same advanced level in 3-5 years of learning Japanese part-time. This is when you can get jobs that require native-level Japanese skills, like interpreters, translators, customer service, and Japanese teachers.

In most cases, the amount of exposure to the Japanese language and culture plays a big part in truly reaching an advanced level. At this point, it’s not just about knowing a lot of grammar points, vocabulary, or kanji; it’s also about understanding the culture and context in which the language is used.
Ways to Speed up Japanese Learning

Most of us have different learning preferences, like taking notes, using visuals or graphics, or speaking words out loud. There are numerous ways to acquire proficiency in Japanese, but selecting the most effective method for yourself will enable you to enhance your learning speed and quality. Here are a few tips we always recommend to those who are starting to learn Japanese.
1. Find a language partner

Studying alone can be boring unless you’re an introvert. Not only does it provide an opportunity to practice speaking and listening in a natural setting, but it also offers insight into Japanese culture, values, and customs. Interacting with native speakers can expose you to a variety of regional dialects, idiomatic expressions, and slang that are not commonly found in textbooks or language courses. Moreover, it allows you to receive immediate feedback on your language usage, pronunciation, and grammar, which is invaluable in accelerating your language acquisition.

Engaging in conversations with Japanese friends or exchange partners can also make language learning more enjoyable, provide new social connections, and lead to a deeper understanding and appreciation of Japanese culture. We recommend checking out our curated list of Japanese language exchange apps and where to find language exchange events.
2. Study Japanese in Japan for Total Immersion

This one is probably obvious, but hear us out: you learn Japanese most effectively when you’re studying the language in Japan — or at least when you are constantly exposed to Japanese culture. Besides, what better way to reward yourself for your hard work than to visit a country we all love?

Immersing yourself in Japanese culture and making friends with native speakers can be almost impossible outside Japan. Being in Japan will boost your progress considerably. You’re conditioned to always use Japanese, and you’ll inevitably hear Japanese words and phrases every day.
3. Define your motivation and goal

Want to learn Japanese as a hobby? Find new job opportunities in Japan from overseas? Watch your favorite anime. It’s good to define your goal in learning Japanese for a couple of reasons; the first being that these goals are your motivators. A lot of people lose interest in learning Japanese because it gets too hard or boring. Knowing why you want to study in the first place helps you to keep the traction going.

Second, and probably more importantly, it helps you identify which language element you need to focus on. Learning Japanese to take the JLPT for university entrance? You should do a well-balanced study plan covering listening, speaking, reading, and vocabulary. Want to be able to make small talk? Try to do more conversation practice instead.
4. Use a mix of Japanese study materials

Perhaps you’re an auditory learner. Or maybe you notice you hate using textbooks. No matter what kind of Japanese learner you are, studying Japanese can be more effective when you’re genuinely enjoying it — or even making it fun!

And the good news is, you can learn from things you already enjoy in Japanese. For example, if you like playing video games, you can switch the language to Japanese, especially with games like Pokémon, where the language is simple and easy to change when starting a new game.

Enjoy reading manga? Challenge yourself to read a bit each day in Japanese, and as you progress, it will become easier. Additionally, watching your favorite shows in Japanese, like anime series or Terrace House on Netflix, is a fun way to pick up new vocabulary and slang. Initially, try watching without subtitles and actively listening, taking notes, and then watching again with subtitles on to see what you understood and learned.
We have a huge list of articles dedicated to different learning resources: Anki, podcasts, YouTube, TikToks and TV shows, so check them out on our blog!
5. Join a Japanese course
It’s important not to overlook the significance of getting the right professional support and establishing a study routine. This is where taking a Japanese course comes in.

One of the main benefits of taking a Japanese class is having access to a qualified instructor who can answer questions, provide feedback, and offer guidance tailored to your individual needs. Additionally, studying with a group of peers can create a sense of accountability and motivation, as well as the opportunity to practice speaking and listening skills with others.

If you’re considering taking a Japanese class, we recommend checking out Coto Academy. They offer a wide range of courses, from beginner to advanced levels, taught by experienced and knowledgeable instructors. Their curriculum is designed to be engaging and interactive, and they use a variety of teaching methods to cater to different learning styles. Additionally, their flexible scheduling options and online classes make it easy to fit language learning into your busy schedule.

Conclusion

Learning to speak Japanese involves many factors, but by developing good study habits, managing your time effectively, and staying committed, you can become conversational in a few months. This may come as a surprise, as you may have had different expectations about the process of learning Japanese.

It’s important to find joy and a sense of satisfaction throughout your journey, not just at the end goal. Celebrate each small accomplishment along the way and try not to focus too much on how far you still have to go. One day, you’ll be glad that you persevered and didn’t give up!
